TradeHQ — Free Paper Trading Simulator

Practice simulated trading across 170 assets with $100,000 in virtual cash. No real money is involved. Learn order mechanics, portfolio tracking, and risk concepts across stocks, crypto, ETFs, forex and commodities.
What TradeHQ actually is

TradeHQ is a free paper-trading simulator for people learning how markets work. Every account starts with $100,000 in virtual cash. Nothing on the site touches real money: there is no brokerage account, no deposit, no withdrawal and no order ever reaches an exchange. Supported holdings use periodically refreshed provider quotes. Unsupported assets can use fixed simulator prices, and charts may show synthetic practice candles. Price and chart labels explain their source and freshness.

A practice account lets you examine decisions without putting savings at risk. For example, compare how different quantities change a hypothetical loss, or record why you changed an exit plan. These exercises do not establish why most beginners lose money or guarantee that practice changes later behaviour.
What you can do here
Paper trade 170 instruments across stocks, crypto, ETFs, forex and commodities using market orders.
Track a full practice portfolio — open positions, realised and unrealised P&L, maximum drawdown, open-position P&L dispersion and allocation snapshots.
Explore four bundled course tracks (options, futures, macroeconomics and decision behaviour) and additional approved catalog releases, with quizzes and completion badges.
Read a 49-term trading glossary written in plain language, each entry with a detailed explanation and a worked example.
Follow step-by-step guides for individual assets, side-by-side asset comparisons, and named strategy walkthroughs.
Keep a trading journal, build daily streaks with the daily challenge, and run a 30-day practice duel against a friend.
Who it is for, and who it is not for

TradeHQ is built for beginners and self-directed learners who want a place to rehearse market mechanics and a repeatable process without using real money. It can also be useful in classroom or independent-study settings.

It is not for you if you want signals, copy-trading, portfolio management, or someone to tell you what to buy. We do not publish price targets, we do not run a Discord with calls, and we do not accept payment for coverage of any asset. If you are looking for a recommendation, this is the wrong site.
Ways to begin learning
Open the markets page and pick one instrument you already recognise.
Read its available educational notes and distinguish identified facts from hypotheses about price changes.
Compare fictional quantities and price changes to understand their effect on a virtual account.
Record the assumptions and limitations of the selected worksheet.
Review what the example illustrates at a time that suits your schedule; no transaction is required.
What educational simulation can and cannot show

Fictional examples can explain market mechanics without requiring a real transaction. Practice does not guarantee profit or replace independent education. A beginner can practice buying and selling holdings with virtual capital, then review those decisions without risking savings. TradeHQ currently supports market orders only; it does not simulate resting limit orders or short positions.
A simulator does not reproduce the financial or personal consequences of a real loss. A written record can support review, but no pattern of participation establishes the quality of future decisions.
Common questions
Is TradeHQ free? Yes, entirely. There is no paid tier, no trial and no card required.

Do I need an account? No. Practice trading, courses and the glossary work without signing up. An optional account supports profiles and community features. Account cash, positions and server-recorded trades restore across devices when available; earlier guest trade history and journals remain on the original browser, while signed-in lessons and journey progress can sync privately when online.
Is the money real? No. Every balance, order and result is simulated, and the platform holds no funds.

Are the prices real? Supported assets use periodically refreshed provider observations. Unsupported assets can use fixed simulator prices; charts may be synthetic. Check each source and timestamp rather than assuming a continuous exchange feed.

Does TradeHQ execute investments or provide personalized advice? No. Trading examples and educational indicator labels are illustrative, not personal recommendations, and the simulator places virtual orders only.

Where is my data? Guest practice records stay in your browser. Signed-in cash, positions and server-recorded trades are stored in Supabase and restored when the service is available. Guest trade history, journal entries and streaks remain browser-held; signed-in lessons and journey progress can sync privately. A badge count alone is not the complete course record.

Paper Trade 170 Assets
Choose from 170 simulated assets and practise placing buy or sell orders. Every account starts with $100,000 in virtual cash. Educational simulation — no real money and no brokerage relationship.
How the practice trading desk works

Choose an instrument, side and quantity to preview a market practice order. Guest orders use the browser's virtual execution input and are recorded in that browser. For signed-in orders, the server selects an eligible quote at execution, so the fill price may differ from the estimate. Account cash, positions and server-recorded trade history restore across devices when the service is available.

The desk supports market practice orders only. A signed-in order may pause if an eligible quote is unavailable. The glossary explains limit and stop orders. Learners choose their own quantities and compare hypothetical exposure to practise the arithmetic. The simplified fill model does not validate real-market risk management.
What to practise on the desk

Position sizing: compare hypothetical quantities under the same adverse price move. A fixed fraction does not guarantee a smoother equity curve, and the current simulator does not execute automatic stop orders.
Exit assumptions: compare the stated hypothetical price with alternative observations; an assumption is not a resting order.
Entry timing: note the price you intended versus the price you received on a fast-moving instrument, and record the gap in the journal.
Concentration: compare otherwise identical hypothetical portfolios with different holdings and state the assumptions.
Limits of any simulator

TradeHQ applies a fixed 0.1% virtual fee to each simulated buy or sell, but that classroom input is not a real broker's fee schedule. Simplified practice fills do not reproduce real-world spreads, slippage, overnight financing or taxes; practice also lacks the emotional weight of risking your own money. Treat results as evidence about your practice process, not a forecast of live returns. Past simulated performance does not predict future real-world performance.
Orders supported by this simulator

The market practice order shows a price estimate. Signed-in fills use an eligible quote at execution. Real market orders seek execution at available prices and may fill at different prices or not complete during market interruptions.
Limit orders appear in the learning material. The current simulator supports market practice orders only.
Closing a position: sell some or all of an existing holding. You cannot sell more than you hold or open a short position. Completed buys and sells appear in portfolio trade history.
Optional review of fictional examples
Choose an exercise with a stated question, record the assumptions before placing orders and review the result afterwards. Transaction count alone does not measure learning or validate a strategy.

A sample journal can ask whether the observed virtual quantity matched the written assumption, what changed after the quoted timestamp and which execution costs are missing. A journal helps review choices but does not establish improved returns.

Practice Markets — Stocks, Crypto, ETFs, Forex | TradeHQ
Browse 170 simulated markets across stocks, crypto, ETFs, forex and commodities. Practice trading with $100,000 virtual cash — free, no signup.
Markets Overview

Browse 170 simulated markets across major asset classes. Explore movers, sentiment-style indicators and sector groupings, then practise with $100,000 virtual cash. This page uses generated display data for education, not live market observations.
What is on the markets page

The markets page lists every instrument available in the simulator, grouped by asset class: US equities, cryptocurrencies, exchange-traded funds, major and minor forex pairs, and commodities. Each row shows a generated practice price and practice change, and links to a dedicated page for that instrument. Changes are seeded initially and then describe the latest generated update, not a measured daily return.

The Markets page uses simulated practice prices and estimated changes for visual feedback. Provider-backed, delayed or cached data may appear elsewhere on TradeHQ and is labelled separately when available. This is a learning environment, not a market-data terminal — do not use these quotes for any real decision.
How to choose what to practise first
Start with something you already understand as a customer or user — a retailer, an index ETF, or a currency you have actually spent.
The generated list cannot measure actual liquidity or spreads; study those concepts separately using dated reference material.
Choose a manageable set of instruments and record what each exercise tests. No fixed study period establishes competence.
Use the linked educational notes to distinguish an instrument's definition from uncertain explanations of price changes.
Asset classes explained briefly
Stocks: fractional ownership of a listed company; move on earnings, guidance, sector rotation and rates.
ETFs: funds with stated holdings and objectives. Diversification, concentration, leverage and product structure affect risk.
Crypto: digital assets traded on venues with varying operating schedules, liquidity and risks. No fixed volatility or price relationship is implied.
Forex: relative pricing of two currencies; central-bank announcements, economic data and other conditions are possible research topics.
Commodities: exposures linked to physical goods, supply, demand and seasonal conditions. Company earnings and equity prices can also have seasonal influences.
Reading a market list without being misled

A percentage move needs a clearly stated interval, observation source and comparison sample. A 3% move can have different meanings for different instruments and periods; it is not a permanent volatility category. Generated practice changes do not establish a real-market daily range.

Volume describes trading activity when it is supplied by a valid market-data source. It does not establish the identity or intentions of buyers and sellers, or prove that a price move will continue or reverse. Simulated or unavailable volume cannot confirm an actual market event.
Things that trip beginners on a markets screen
Assuming a large recent gain predicts the next price move; an observed change does not determine future returns or a suitable entry.
Assuming a low nominal price alone establishes whether an asset is inexpensive; the units and method of valuation matter.
Treating any ETF as automatically low-risk: sector funds and concentrated funds still carry market and holding-specific risks.
Ignoring market hours: equities gap overnight, crypto trades continuously, forex has session-driven liquidity.

Your Practice Portfolio — Positions, P&L, Analytics | TradeHQ
Track simulated positions, realised and unrealised P&L, max drawdown, open-position P&L dispersion and allocation snapshots.
Practice Portfolio

Review simulated positions, trades, P&L, drawdown and allocation snapshots. Guest records stay in your browser; account cash, positions and server-recorded trades restore when the service is available. Server-recorded account trades restore across devices; earlier guest history and journals remain browser-held.
What the practice portfolio tracks

The portfolio page shows open positions with entry prices, current practice prices and unrealised profit or loss, plus eligible recorded transaction history. Guest records live in local storage. Signed-in cash, positions and server-recorded transactions can restore when the service is available; clearing browser data does not delete that account copy. Earlier guest records and journals remain browser-held.

Beyond raw P&L, the page calculates fee-inclusive closed-result win rate, average win versus average loss, current open-position return dispersion, and practice maximum drawdown. These summarize recorded outcomes and exposures that can help you review your practice process. The chart can include generated history; it is not a verified sequence of account observations.
How to read your own numbers honestly
Compare win rate, average realized win, average realized loss and costs together. A high win rate alone does not establish a positive result.
Maximum drawdown describes a selected peak-to-trough decline. It does not measure every risk or predict your response to a real loss.
A short run is an observation, not proof of a repeatable advantage. Selection, dependence, costs and changing conditions matter; no fixed trade count establishes an edge.
If one position contributes most of a measured result, that observation alone cannot establish the effect of a method.
Why results here do not transfer one-to-one

The simulator applies a 0.1% practice transaction fee, rather than a real broker fee schedule. It does not model financing costs, taxes or actual market execution. Review practice results alongside these limits; they do not predict real-money results.
The metrics explained in plain language

Unrealised P&L: the difference between an open position's current marked value and its cost basis. Closing a position records realised P&L using its actual recorded proceeds and cost basis, which can differ from the earlier mark. All balances and results here remain virtual.
Realised P&L: the result of trades you have actually closed. It is an accounting result, not a measure of decision quality.
Open positions in profit: the share of current open positions showing positive unrealised P&L. This is not a closed-trade win rate.
Open-position P&L dispersion: the spread of current position returns around their average. This is a snapshot, not a Sharpe ratio or time-series volatility measure.

Practice maximum drawdown: the largest fall from a peak in locally stored snapshots, which can include generated hourly backfill. It is not an observed market record or proof that a strategy is survivable.
Reviewing the portfolio weekly

Choose a repeatable review interval for virtual results and compare the information recorded before each order with what became known later. A loss alone cannot establish whether the original reasoning was sound.
Compare the largest virtual gain with its position size, price change, quotation source and costs. A large one-off outcome does not by itself establish skill or predict a similar future result.

Start Here — Beginner Practice Trading Journey | TradeHQ
Learn how virtual trading works, practise an order, understand its costs, review your portfolio and continue with daily exercises.
Your First Virtual Trade, Explained

Try an optional Daily Practice scenario, then follow five guided steps to understand an order, place a voluntary simulated trade, review cash and holdings, reflect, and choose what to learn next. No account or real money is required.
Step 1 — Understand an order before placing one

The optional Daily Practice scenario comes first. In the guided lesson that follows, compare a displayed quote with the execution price. Consider two fictional shares showing $50 each. Their quoted purchase value is $100, and a 0.1% simulated fee adds $0.10. The estimated debit is therefore $100.10, assuming a $50 fill. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's Investor.gov guidance explains that a real market order's execution price is not guaranteed by the last quote. The simulator is simpler, and must not be mistaken for a live brokerage.

The learner answers a short understanding check before entering the trading desk. The exercise presents an invented scenario for reading costs and uncertainty, not a stock recommendation or a return promise.
Steps 2 and 3 — Place a voluntary virtual trade, then inspect the numbers

Before opening the main virtual trading terminal, learners can optionally try a five-round fictional Practice Arena warm-up covering cash, holdings and a model fee. The warm-up's invented prices and browser-local balances are separate from the $100,000 trading portfolio, do not enter leaderboards, and do not advance the five-step journey. It can be skipped at any time; an Arena completion is not a saved guided trade.

The guided link opens the normal virtual trading terminal, optionally selecting an illustrative asset. It never places an order on the learner's behalf. The visitor chooses a quantity and explicitly confirms any simulated transaction. A successful saved trade advances the journey; merely pressing a guide button does not.

The next stage reads the learner's actual saved practice data. It shows remaining virtual cash, total account value, number of holdings, and the chosen trade's quantity, execution price, calculated fee and cash movement. Open-position returns change with the available reference price and are not guaranteed cash profits. A refreshed or delayed quote can differ from an earlier reference.
Steps 4 and 5 — Reflect and return for daily practice

Learners write a private reflection explaining what surprised them about the price or fee and what they will check before another exercise. New reflection text stays in the browser even when signed in. Only the completed step can sync with the account. Older reflections that already synced remain private. TradeHQ then recommends a risk-management lesson and the existing Daily Practice exercises; completion does not certify readiness to risk real money.

The journey records completed steps in browser storage so guest visitors can return later on the same browser. Signed-in members can also privately sync supported lessons, quiz drafts, reading position and journey progress between devices when online. A course's most-recent-lesson record helps resume the right lesson. Clearing guest browser data can remove that guest's progress; portfolio backups do not include learning records.
What a first practice result can and cannot show

A fictional profit or loss is useful for checking arithmetic, exposure, and whether the learner understood their own decision. It does not reproduce real transaction liquidity, bid/ask spreads, slippage, tax obligations or the consequences of risking money. A short winning streak is not evidence of an investing skill. The intended result of this lesson is a better explanation of the order and its limitations, not a trade signal.

Learn to Trade — Free Lessons, Guides & Glossary | TradeHQ
Free trading lessons, glossary, and step-by-step guides for beginners. Learn stocks, crypto and technical analysis, then practice with $100,000 virtual cash.
Learn to Trade

Structured lessons, a 49-term glossary, and long-form guides on stocks, crypto, ETFs and technical analysis. Supported spot mechanics can be explored in the simulator; derivatives and unsupported indicators use separate conceptual worksheets.
Two different ways to learn here

TradeHQ separates learning into two formats on purpose. Full courses organize related topics into multi-lesson tracks with quizzes, source notes and completion badges. Quick reads address narrower questions. Neither format certifies complete mastery.

Both formats link to the virtual practice desk. Reading explains concepts; a simulated order can illustrate the arithmetic and interface, but the resulting virtual performance cannot validate financial competence.
A suggested order for complete beginners
Use the beginner practice guide to learn what virtual orders, prices and fees mean, then follow a structured course for more detail.
Use the trading psychology course to examine records, decisions and bias; it does not assign a universal cause to beginner losses.
Use the macro course to read releases and distinguish observed information from uncertain explanations of price changes.
Study the options and futures lessons as conceptual examples of contracts, leverage and risk; TradeHQ does not execute real or simulated derivative contracts.
Keep the glossary open in a second tab and look up every unfamiliar term as it appears.
How this material is written and reviewed

Lessons are designed for independent study. Relevant sources accompany many definitions and examples, while some references are background rather than evidence of a strategy's effectiveness. Numerical scenarios are illustrative, not forecasts or individual financial recommendations. Report missing or misleading citations through the Contact page.
What a realistic learning timeline looks like

Learning timelines differ with prior knowledge, study time and the task being practised. A calendar duration does not establish proficiency or investment readiness. Set an observable learning goal, such as explaining an order fill or reproducing a fee calculation, and record which parts remain uncertain.

For a concrete self-check, write down a quote price, quantity and the simulator's 0.1% fee, calculate the virtual purchase cost, then compare your result with the practice order panel. If the figures differ, inspect quantity, rounding and quote freshness before moving on. Completing this exercise checks one skill, not overall investing readiness.
How to tell good trading education from bad
Good material explains mechanics and probability; bad material promises returns.
Good material shows losing examples; bad material only shows winners.
Check whether a source actually supports the claim. A primary document can provide useful evidence; a screenshot without verifiable context is insufficient on its own.
Good material tells you who it is not for; bad material claims to suit everyone.
A credible educational source separates observations from forecasts, documents data limitations and does not use time pressure as evidence.

Beginner Trading Practice Guide | TradeHQ
Study simulated market orders, fees, price observations and record-keeping, with $100,000 in virtual practice funds. Not a complete investing course.
Beginner Trading Practice Guide

An introduction to the virtual practice dashboard, order mechanics and a worked buy/sell-fee example. Links to longer courses and reference material; $100,000 is simulated money, not an investment account.
What this page actually provides

This page is a starting map and interactive practice dashboard, not a complete textbook or independently tested trading course. It introduces quote reading, simulated market orders, fees and reviewing hypothetical outcomes. Use the linked structured courses for deeper explanations of instruments, order types and portfolio concepts. The exercises illustrate arithmetic and questions to ask, not a profitable strategy.
Four checks for a virtual practice exercise
Exposure: quantify the share of virtual cash used and calculate what a chosen adverse price change would do to the holding.
Exit assumptions: write down both a higher and a lower hypothetical sale price. TradeHQ does not support resting limit or stop orders.
Observation quality: record the quote source, timestamp, asset and quote currency. A generated chart need not reproduce traded market history.
Review: retain the original assumptions, both virtual fees and alternative outcomes. One or ten practice results do not establish a repeatable advantage.
Worked example: virtual shares, fees and two outcomes

Assume a purely hypothetical purchase of ten shares at $50 each. The gross cost is $500 and a 0.1% virtual purchase fee is $0.50, so the total cash used is $500.50. If the assumed sale price is $46, the gross proceeds are $460 and a 0.1% virtual sale fee is $0.46; net proceeds are $459.54. Compared with the original $500.50 cost, the round trip produces a loss of $40.96.

For the same ten shares, a separate hypothetical sale at $54 yields $540 gross, less a $0.54 virtual sale fee, or $539.46 net. Subtract the $500.50 initial cost to get a gain of $38.96. These prices are invented, not a forecast or observed fills. Actual transactions can involve spreads, slippage, taxes and other costs not captured here.
What this simulator cannot teach by itself

TradeHQ offers virtual market orders, not real brokerage transactions, short positions or resting limit/stop orders. Even when a displayed quote comes from an external provider, a simulated fill does not establish that the same price or liquidity would be available on an exchange.

Use the structured courses and linked sources to check concepts rather than treating a synthetic sentiment label, an indicator, or a hypothetical growth calculator as a verified trading signal. Practice outcomes do not predict real-money results.
The vocabulary you need before anything else
Bid and ask: at a given time, the best displayed bid and ask are quoted buying and selling prices. Their difference is the spread. Actual fills and costs can differ from that snapshot.
Liquidity: the availability of buyers and sellers at prices and quantities. Limited liquidity can make a real order harder or more costly to execute.
Volatility: a measure of price variation over a stated period. It describes past movement; it cannot dictate one universally appropriate exit level or position size.

Leverage: exposure larger than posted funds through borrowing or derivatives. Gains and losses can be magnified, and collateral or liquidation rules vary by product and venue. TradeHQ does not provide leverage.

Expectancy example, not a forecast: five hypothetical wins of $30 and five losses of $20 total $50 before costs. Ten $2 round-trip fees reduce that to $30 net. This invented ten-trade record is too small and artificial to establish a repeatable advantage.
A first-month plan
Week one: label the bid, ask, spread and quote time on an example, then inspect virtual market orders without using real funds.
Week two: write assumptions before a virtual example, including quantity, fee, possible lower sale price and an alternative outcome.
Week three: check each recorded virtual outcome against its original assumptions; distinguish a mark from an executable real-world quote.
Week four: compare the journal entries for missing costs, changed assumptions and hindsight bias. Note what the simulation cannot test.

Trader Leaderboard

New accounts start private and can opt into public visibility. Public members are eligible without a minimum trade count; the board requests up to 500 records. Comparable portfolios receive practice ranks after their first server-recorded trade. Held asset prices are refreshed in the background, with quote age and simulation labels. Previous browser-reported results are labelled separately from current rankings; practice results are not audited investment returns.
What the leaderboard shows

Public practice profiles can appear without a minimum trade count. The current board requests up to 500 current member records. Comparable portfolios receive numbered practice ranks after their first server-recorded trade, ordered by simulated return. Unranked members appear separately. New accounts start private and may opt in to public visibility from their profile. Values use a $100,000 virtual starting balance and display quote freshness and simulation status.
There is no prize, no fee and no real money involved. Use the scoreboard as a prompt to review exposure, costs and assumptions; rank alone does not measure a reliable method.
How to read a ranking without fooling yourself
A large return over a handful of trades is insufficient evidence of skill; inspect exposure and the full record.
Compare drawdown alongside return where comparable records exist. Neither statistic alone measures method reliability.
Short windows can hide adverse paths and sample uncertainty. Compare consistent periods before drawing a conclusion.
Nobody's practice ranking is a recommendation to copy their trades.
Why we show it at all

The practice board provides an optional comparison of simulated records. A ranking can prompt a discussion about exposure and assumptions, but no improvement in habits or financial results is established by participation. There is no reward.

Ranked practice uses server-recorded orders. Previous results preserve earlier browser-reported summaries separately, with their last-reported date. They do not enter current rankings and are not verified investment returns.
Privacy on the leaderboard
New accounts start private. Only profiles that their owners explicitly make public show selected profile fields and simulated statistics.
Public board entries may show your chosen username, country if supplied, selected virtual statistics and separately enabled eligible trophy flair. Email addresses are not displayed by the board.
Switching to private hides the entry from new leaderboard requests; already open pages reflect changes when refreshed.
Frequently asked
Do I have to appear here? No. New profiles start private, and you may opt into public visibility at any time from your profile page.
Is there a prize? No. There is no money, no entry fee and nothing to win.

Can I see someone's trades? Only if that member independently opts in to showing recent current-cycle server-recorded practice orders on an otherwise public profile. Private journal entries and browser-only history never appear.

How often does it update? Held assets are checked in the background every five minutes, with traditional instruments rotating through a limited batch. The visible board refreshes every minute. Provider delays and outages can leave older quotes; unsupported assets use fixed simulator prices.

Who appears? Public members, including accounts without trades, are eligible; the current board requests up to 500 records. Only comparable server-recorded portfolios receive practice ranks after a first trade; imported portfolios stay unranked.

Trading Mentor — Curated Knowledge

Ask the mentor about trading concepts. This chat uses a built-in answer library and local topic matching, with no AI API request. Answers can miss your question and are educational only. Practice what you learn on the free simulator with $100,000 virtual cash.
What the rule-based mentor does

This chat matches your question to a built-in library of educational answers about trading concepts, indicators and order types. It does not call a language model, read your journal or assess a proposed investment. Separate portfolio mentor tools can use the simulated figures shown on that page.
What it will not do
It does not give buy or sell recommendations, price targets or personalised financial advice.
It does not know your real financial circumstances and cannot assess suitability.
Authored answers and topic matching can be wrong or miss the question. Check important claims against a primary source.
It is not a substitute for a licensed professional in your own jurisdiction.
Getting useful answers

Ask about mechanics rather than what to buy. Try a supported topic such as risk/reward, diversification or dollar-cost averaging. Topic matching may return a general answer or miss your intent; it does not provide a personalised suitability assessment. Derivatives lessons are conceptual because this simulator does not trade options or futures contracts.
Good questions to ask it
Explain what happens to a call option's value if the stock does not move for two weeks.
What is the difference between a stop-loss order and a stop-limit order, and when does each fail?
My practice win rate is 60% but I am down overall — what does that imply about my exits?
Why do forex pairs move on interest-rate announcements?
Explain the distinction between a fictional holding's marked value and the total account value.
How it works and what it costs

The mentor uses a built-in library of authored educational answers, topic matching and calculations. Chat does not call an AI provider or use AI credits. Its coverage is limited to the available topics; an unfamiliar question may receive a general explanation rather than a tailored answer.

Mentor topic matching happens in your browser and does not send the conversation to an AI provider. Advertising and analytics are separate services described in the privacy policy. Educational answers can still contain mistakes or omit context; check substantive claims against a primary source before relying on them.
A reminder about limits

No assistant, however fluent, can assess whether a trade suits your finances, and none of the answers here are regulated advice. Treat the mentor as a patient tutor for mechanics and vocabulary, and take anything that sounds like a recommendation as a sign the question needs rewording.

Daily Trading Challenge — Build Your Streak | TradeHQ
A fictional daily scenario plus an optional 10-question case study with labelled visuals and worked explanations. 50 exercises rotate and may repeat.
Daily Trading Challenge

Practise a quick scenario or go deeper with a hypothetical case, labelled visual, 10 linked questions and worked explanations. 50 exercises rotate; new banks are targeted every two months and require owner approval. Answers stay on this browser.
How the daily challenge works

Daily offers a quick hypothetical market scenario alongside a longer ten-question case study. You choose a response, compare the reasoning and trade-offs, then answer a short bonus knowledge question about market basics. Completing the quick reasoning step or all ten case-study questions advances the browser-stored streak at most once per local day. Directional reflections are not forecast scores.

The scenario's prices, news events and dates are exercise inputs, not a report of what happened in today's markets. Choosing long, short or hold records a reflection; it does not place an order. Use the explanation to compare assumptions and uncertainty rather than treating completion as evidence of forecasting skill.
Using a daily habit to support review
Review the reasoning and arithmetic when it is useful; no particular frequency establishes skill.
A short exercise is optional. Choose a study interval that fits your schedule.
A streak counts participation; it does not establish that a particular study habit has formed.
After a missed day, resume when your schedule allows; a streak is a participation aid, not a skill grade.
A longer daily practice session

The deeper exercise develops one case across ten linked questions, so the learner can calculate an input, interpret the result and identify a limitation. Topics rotate between portfolio arithmetic, transaction costs and supported orders, price-data freshness, risk and uncertainty, and decision habits. The visuals show selected hypothetical inputs with numeric labels; they are not live market charts. Worked explanations appear after each submitted answer, including when the answer was wrong.

After you finish, the case takeaway provides a review guide for checking the reasoning. Checked answers are saved on this browser. After the first saved answer, the case keeps its own snapshot if a new bank is approved while you are working. Clearing site data removes this local history; an account does not synchronize this case history to another device.

The configured generation workflow targets a new 50-exercise bank every two calendar months in five parts using the configured Gemini API. A target schedule is not a publication guarantee. Each completed bank remains private and editable in the owner’s admin panel until final review and approval. If generation hits a quota limit, fails validation or awaits review, the approved bank continues rotating. Fifty exercises can therefore repeat before the next bank begins; revisits are review practice rather than a claim of brand-new daily content. The feature does not use a paid provider fallback.
What the challenges cover
A hypothetical market scenario with stated exercise inputs, rather than current market news.

Practice Arena — Interactive Virtual Trading Decisions | TradeHQ
Practise five fictional trading decisions in minutes. Reveal price changes, see virtual cash and fees, and review your reasoning. Free, private, no signup.
TradeHQ Practice Arena

Practice Arena is a free, self-contained interactive training exercise. Choose a beginner or intermediate scenario, observe deliberately fictional prices, and decide whether to buy a small exercise position, sell already held units or wait. Each decision reveals another invented observation and explains the accounting and assumptions. The Arena begins with its own $10,000 fictional cash ledger. The model charges a 0.1% fee on virtual buys and sells, and records exercise choices privately in this browser. It never places an order on TradeHQ's normal virtual trading terminal, changes a user portfolio, alters a public leaderboard, or consults a real-market quote. A favorable exercise result cannot establish trading competence or forecast real performance. After reviewing a scenario, continue with the beginner journey, risk lesson or deeper Daily Practice.
How Practice Arena works

Practice Arena is an interactive training exercise built around deliberate choices rather than trading predictions. Choose one of three authored paths: Your First Decision, Size Changes Everything, or Stay With the Plan. Each path contains five small decision rounds. The next hypothetical observation is hidden until you choose to buy a fictional unit, sell units you already hold, or wait without making an order. This helps you practise noticing assumptions without claiming that a particular price direction is objectively correct.

All instruments and prices in the Arena are invented classroom examples. They are not historical exchange observations, live quotes, market forecasts or recommendations to buy or sell any real security. A user can enter the exercise without an account, paying a fee or connecting a brokerage. The separate practice balance begins with 10,000 fictional dollars for the purposes of these specific decisions. This is not the main TradeHQ simulator's 100,000-dollar balance, and nothing in the Arena sends an order to the main trading terminal.
A worked illustration of the virtual ledger

Imagine a fictional asset displayed at $100 a unit, an exercise cash balance of $10,000 and an order to purchase one unit. The classroom calculation uses the purchase notional of $100 plus a 0.1% transaction fee of $0.10. Exercise cash becomes $9,899.90 and the held unit is initially worth $100 at the same fictional mark, leaving marked equity of $9,999.90. The decrease is the modelled fee, not the loss of the entire purchase value.

If the next invented observation is $102, the one held unit is marked at $102 and the combined exercise equity would be $10,001.90. If a user simply observes instead of buying, no units are purchased or sold, cash stays unchanged and no transaction fee is charged. A sale is allowed only for units actually held; a user cannot open a short position in this teaching exercise. Costs and changes are displayed immediately after each decision. These examples describe arithmetic, not actual exchange settlement, liquidity, taxes or execution.
Why the Arena asks for a reason

Before revealing the next scenario observation, you may write what you are trying to test or why you would prefer to observe without placing an order. Afterward, the review panel compares the recorded action with the next invented mark, the modelled fee, remaining cash and the value of any held units. A profitable fictional decision is not declared a good decision, and an unprofitable one is not automatically described as a mistake. The purpose is to examine what is known, what was assumed and how the decision affects the ledger.

The first path focuses on basic cash and fee accounting, the second on the dollar effect of position quantity, and the intermediate path on distinguishing evidence from unsupported claims under changing conditions. The next step can be an existing beginner journey, a risk-management lesson or a deeper Daily Practice case. The three paths are finite and can be repeated; TradeHQ does not advertise unlimited new historical market scenarios.

After completing five rounds, the review separates the value effect of fictional price changes from the virtual fees charged for buying or selling. The price effect includes changes in units still held, so it is not necessarily a realized trading result. Learners can expand a chronological record of every decision and its optional stated reason, then write a private closing reflection about what to test again. This information remains on their device.

The optional usefulness prompt lets a learner choose whether an exercise was useful, confusing or too easy. Choosing an option does not transmit it. If a learner explicitly opens the Contact page, TradeHQ can prefill an email draft that they may edit and decide whether to send. Selecting a usefulness response does not automatically submit the response. Separate performance and optional analytics requests are described in the Privacy Policy.
Privacy, limitations and what the result means

Arena exercises use intentionally fictional prices and an isolated local ledger. They never change the signed-in practice portfolio, guest simulator balance, public rankings or verified competition records.
Decisions, optional notes and completion history stay in the same browser. Clearing site data may erase them, and signing in does not currently synchronize Arena sessions across devices.
The exercise does not simulate market spreads, order-book depth, slippage, broker regulation, borrowing, stop execution, tax costs or the emotional consequences of risking real savings.
A finished session is a record of educational participation, not investment advice, a skill certification, a personalized trading recommendation or evidence of likely real financial returns.
Visitors can leave without making a trade. Waiting is a deliberate choice and carries no fictional transaction fee.

Optional Arena usage milestones use Amplitude only after an adult visitor confirms they are at least 18 and explicitly accepts the renewed analytics choice; no prior acceptance is reused. Replay and automatic interactions are disabled in the website analytics setup. These events can indicate a start, completion, resume or later same-browser visit, but do not transmit decisions, balances, portfolio identities or written reflections. Rejecting analytics does not disable the simulator. A five-minute voluntary study offers before-and-after concept questions and optional feedback; the answers stay in the current page until the participant explicitly copies or prepares an email, and no message is sent automatically.

Challenge a Friend

Create a shareable invite for a 30-day practice duel. Each participant is measured from their own recorded starting value, using server-recorded trades and deadline-frozen simulated scores. Educational simulation only.
How a practice duel works

An optional practice duel requires public profiles for creation and joining. Both starting values are recorded when the invitation is accepted; the values can differ. While the applicable profiles are public, other visitors can view eligible duel records and scores, not only the invited participant. Making a profile private restricts new public access, while participants may retain access. The page shows a 30-day countdown and compares server-recorded simulated percentage changes. Final scores use trades and the last cached valuation quotes available at the deadline and are then frozen. Older client-summary duels are labelled legacy because reliable final values cannot be recovered.

Nothing is wagered and nothing is won. There is no entry fee, no prize pool and no real money at any point — this is an optional comparison of simulated records; participation is not required and no improvement in study habits is established.
Rules that make a duel actually useful
For a virtual challenge, agree on the example's quantity and exposure assumptions; TradeHQ does not provide leverage or real-money wagering.
If participants choose to keep a virtual journal, compare stated assumptions and data-source labels rather than treating ranking as a measure of investment ability.
Compare the illustrated drawdowns and simulated returns without claiming they establish superior real-world skill.
Discuss which hypothetical assumptions were missing or changed; there is no prize or real-money outcome.
What a duel does and does not prove

A 30-day simulated result cannot separate skill from luck or predict who would lead over a year. Concentrated exposure can produce large gains or losses. Compare the stated assumptions and drawdowns without inferring a reliable future ranking.
If participants independently choose to discuss their fictional records, they can compare assumptions and limitations. No participation, ranking or journal comparison guarantees learning.

Each participant uses their own recorded starting balance; those balances can differ.
The scoreboard compares percentage changes from recorded starting values. Different exposure, costs and activity can limit comparability.

Privacy Policy

Guest simulator records stay in your browser. Account cash, positions and server-recorded trades are stored with Supabase; account, community and consented analytics features also involve provider processing. See the full policy for details.
Policy update
Last Updated: November 22, 2026
Information TradeHQ Handles
TradeHQ can be used without creating an account. The data handled depends on the features you choose.

• Guest simulator data: practice cash, positions and trade history are stored in your browser with a separate browser-local recovery copy. You can download or explicitly restore a portable practice backup JSON file containing trading history and any private journal notes. The backup feature does not upload this file. Backup formats can be manually edited: TradeHQ validates file structure and arithmetic but does not certify authenticity, investment performance or leaderboard ranking. An imported guest file remains unverified. Guest learning-journey progress, course progress, streaks and related settings remain browser-stored. For signed-in users, lesson completion, unfinished quiz answers, reading position and first-trade journey progress may also be saved privately in Supabase and synchronized across devices when online. New beginner-journey reflection text stays on the device. Older reflections already synchronized remain private in the account. Streaks and unrelated browser preferences are not part of this account sync.
• Signed-in portfolio data: Supabase stores account cash, positions and server-recorded practice orders, including asset, quantity, execution price, fees, time and simulated result. These account records restore across devices when the service is available. Signed-in users can also download a server-signed current-cycle historical practice export and verify its integrity against their authenticated account. This file may contain account identifiers and private transaction details; it is not publicly shared or accepted as an upload that replaces ranked trades. A first-time browser import stores cash and positions as an unranked portfolio; earlier guest trade history stays in its original browser. Starting a fresh ranked practice cycle archives the previous account snapshot privately. Journals remain browser-held; signed-in lesson and beginner-journey progress can sync privately and are not used to determine public trading ranks.
• Optional account data: if you create an account, Supabase processes authentication data such as your email or provider identity and can store profile fields including username, country and bio.
• Foundations assessments and certificates: when a signed-in learner uses the optional Foundations programme, Supabase stores account-linked assessment identifiers, scores, possible points and qualifying learning dates. When a learner requests a certificate, TradeHQ stores the recipient name they provide, the programme and milestone, template version, issue date and qualifying assessment evidence so the same certificate can be retrieved. Name corrections are retained as revision history; an earlier name is not erased simply by correcting it. Optional verification sharing stores a hash of the verification credential and its name revision. A person given a valid verification link can check the programme version, milestone and issue date, not the recipient name or private scores. The learner can withdraw or replace the verification link; correcting the name invalidates the previous link. Account deletion cascades to these account-linked Foundations records. A downloaded PDF or copy shared outside TradeHQ is not removed by withdrawing verification or deleting an account.
• Community data: signed-in features can store selected practice statistics, public-profile settings, reviews and duel/challenge records. A separate setting, OFF by default, lets a member voluntarily disclose up to 20 current-cycle server-recorded simulated trade entries on an otherwise public profile: asset, buy/sell, quantity, execution price, fee and date. The public data response also includes trade total, simulated realised profit/loss where recorded, and price-source information, even when a visible profile row shows fewer fields. Private journals, reflections, past cycles and browser-only records are never shared by this feature. These are simulated results, not brokerage statements or verified real-money performance. Creating or joining a practice duel requires public profiles. Eligible public duel responses include participant identifiers, invite code, recorded starting values, score values and relevant dates; other visitors may read them while the applicable profiles are public. Switching a profile to private restricts new non-participant access under the duel access policy; participants can retain access, and previously viewed copies cannot be recalled.
• Review submissions and interactions: TradeHQ stores your submitted display name (if provided), review text, rating, moderation status and an IP-derived hash used for duplicate prevention. The hash is restricted to authorized backend processing; it is not a public review field. A hash is not necessarily anonymous information. Likes are stored with your account ID and the review ID to enforce one like per account. Public pages show totals, not individual liker identities. Owner replies are public. Reviews removed from public view remain in the private admin panel for restoration. Contact TradeHQ for privacy or removal requests.
• Optional TradeHQ Newsletter: if you explicitly request the educational newsletter, TradeHQ stores your email address, consent/confirmation status, the date and source of signup, unsubscribe status, and delivery receipts in private Supabase records. Resend handles email delivery and receives your address for confirmations and issues. We never add prior contact records to the mailing list without permission. Every newsletter provides an unsubscribe link, and you may use the contact page to request deletion.
• Contact messages: by default the contact page opens your email app or lets you copy a draft into webmail. If the optional direct-send service is configured, Cloudflare Turnstile processes challenge and connection information and Resend processes the message, sender reply address and recipient information to deliver it to the maintainer's inbox. TradeHQ does not retain direct-send message bodies in its application database. The maintainer's email provider retains delivered messages according to its settings.
• Technical data: hosting, authentication, security and abuse-prevention services can receive normal request information such as IP address, browser/device information and server logs.
• Website performance: current pages load Cloudflare Web Analytics to measure page loading and performance. Its browser beacon can send the page URL, a page-load identifier, timing and browser performance measurements to Cloudflare, separately from optional Amplitude events. These performance requests can run before an analytics choice and after Amplitude is rejected. Cloudflare states that its Web Analytics usage metrics do not use cookies, local storage or fingerprinting to track individuals. This does not mean that network requests contain no connection information or that every jurisdiction exempts this processing from privacy requirements.
• Font delivery: pages request stylesheets and font files from Google Fonts. Google receives the connecting IP address, the requested resource URL and request headers, which can include browser/operating-system information and the referring page according to browser settings. These requests are separate from Amplitude consent and may occur before a choice or after rejection. Google states that its Fonts API does not set or log cookies and does not use Fonts information to create end-user profiles or for targeted advertising.
• Optional analytics and advertising data: TradeHQ offers a newly scoped analytics choice only to visitors affirmatively confirming they are at least 18. This confirmation is for optional analytics; it is not an age restriction on lessons, guest practice or sign-in. Visitors under 18 should reject optional analytics. If accepted, Amplitude can receive limited Practice Arena milestone events and two leaderboard registration-flow events (an eligible signed-out leaderboard visit, and a newly created account subsequently authenticated in that same browser within seven days), along with its pseudonymous browser identity and ordinary network metadata. The two leaderboard custom events contain no email, account ID, username, profile details, portfolio data, transaction information, or form content. The temporary seven-day same-browser attribution marker stores only a visit timestamp and is cleared on consent rejection or successful attribution. No custom Amplitude events are sent when optional analytics is declined; the website does not claim visitor identity is anonymous. Why a glossary matters more in trading than in most subjects

Trading vocabulary is unusually hostile to beginners because the same word often carries a precise technical meaning and a loose marketing meaning at the same time. 'Leverage' is a neutral description of borrowed exposure in a textbook and a sales pitch in an advertisement. 'Support' is a level where buyers previously appeared, not a floor that holds. Reading material without pinning down which meaning is in play is how people end up confident about something they have misunderstood.

Each entry here therefore gives a plain definition first, then a longer educational explanation of the mechanics, then the practical caveat that matters when you try to use the idea. Where a concept is popular but weakly evidenced, the entry says so instead of repeating the folklore.

Short Squeeze — Explanation & Learning Exercise | TradeHQ Wiki
A short squeeze occurs when a rising price or difficulty borrowing a security puts pressure on short sellers to close positions by buying shares.
Short Squeeze — Trading Wiki

A short squeeze occurs when a rising price or difficulty borrowing a security puts pressure on short sellers to close positions by buying shares. That covering demand can add further upward pressure to the price.
Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. Limited source check: 2026-11-01. Checked short-sale closing mechanics, periodic short-interest snapshots, the days-to-cover formula and 10 × ($28 − $20) = $80 illustrative loss against FINRA sources. No individual squeeze event, predictive signal or historical return series was verified. This is not independent professional review.
In depth

A short seller borrows a security, sells it, and later needs to buy equivalent securities to close the position and return what was borrowed. If the price rises instead of falling, the short position loses value. A short squeeze can develop when price increases or borrowing constraints cause multiple short sellers to cover at the same time; those purchases add demand and can intensify the upward move. Short interest is one useful measure of outstanding short positions, while days to cover compares reported short interest with average daily share volume.

FINRA publishes these measures as market data, but they do not create a universal squeeze threshold or a reliable timing signal. Reported short interest is also a periodic snapshot rather than a real-time count. Borrowing availability, trading volume, price movement, liquidity and the behaviour of market participants can all affect whether heavy short positioning ever becomes a squeeze.
Key points
A squeeze can occur when rising prices or borrowing pressure cause short sellers to cover
Covering purchases can add further upward pressure to the price
Short interest and days to cover provide context but do not define a universal squeeze threshold
Why it matters when you are learning

Treat short interest and days-to-cover figures as context, not a trigger. Compare current reported data with earlier periods and check how the price and trading volume are behaving; no single percentage or ratio guarantees that a squeeze will occur.
Worked exercise and its limits

Hypothetical short-sale worksheet: 10 borrowed shares sold at $20 and repurchased at $28 create an $80 loss before borrowing costs. Explain why buying to cover adds demand, while a price rise alone cannot reveal who bought. TradeHQ cannot open short positions.

Golden Cross — Trading Wiki

A golden cross labels a shorter moving average crossing above a longer one, often the 50-day above the 200-day. It describes historical averages and does not establish that prices will continue rising.
Publisher and editorial transparency
Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.
In depth

A golden cross labels a shorter moving average crossing above a longer one; 50-day and 200-day simple averages are a common convention. Each average summarizes selected past closing prices. The crossover can arrive after a substantial price rise, and a subsequent reversal can produce another crossover. Changing the interval, lookback or price adjustment changes the observations. The label does not reveal institutional orders or establish a profitable entry. For a comparison, state the dataset and rules before reviewing later prices, include failed examples and account for costs.
A generated practice chart cannot establish how a rule performed in real historical markets.
Key points
50-day MA crossing above the 200-day MA is the classic setup
Calculated from past prices; a crossover can lag or reverse
Does not establish future buying activity or a profitable entry
Why it matters when you are learning
The golden cross compares historical averages; the crossover does not establish what price will do next.
Worked exercise and its limits

On a separate historical dataset, mark a 50-period average crossing a 200-period average. Freeze the interval and settings before looking forward; include later failed crosses. TradeHQ's generated candles cannot validate the pattern against real history.

Death Cross — Trading Wiki
A death cross labels a shorter moving average crossing below a longer one, often the 50-day below the 200-day. This is a lagging price calculation, not confirmation of a future decline.
Publisher and editorial transparency
Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.
In depth

A death cross labels a shorter moving average crossing below a longer one, commonly a 50-day average below a 200-day average. It describes the relationship between selected historical averages. It need not identify the beginning of a decline, and a later recovery can reverse the crossover. The slope of either average is another historical observation, not a universal measure of signal strength. Do not infer how professional managers position portfolios from this label. To evaluate an imagined rule, specify the series, frequency, execution assumptions and comparison period before inspecting outcomes.
Include costs and both continuation and recovery cases.
Key points
A 50-day average crossing below a 200-day average fits the conventional definition
A description of selected historical prices, not a validated prediction of a downturn
Compare price and volume observations without assuming confirmation predicts returns
Why it matters when you are learning
Mark when the selected averages cross, then compare later continuations and reversals. Recognising a historical crossover does not guarantee protection from a future decline.
Worked exercise and its limits

Construct two hypothetical paths with the same downward moving-average crossover: one recovers and one continues falling. The common crossover cannot distinguish their futures. Explain the delay caused by averaging old prices.

Liquidation Cascade — Trading Wiki
A liquidation cascade is feedback in which forced position reductions add price pressure that can trigger further reductions. Venue rules, collateral and liquidity affect the outcome.
Publisher and editorial transparency
Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.
In depth

In a leveraged market, falling collateral value or adverse price changes can cause positions to breach maintenance requirements. Forced reductions may add buying or selling pressure. If that pressure worsens prices for other leveraged positions, additional liquidations can follow. Such feedback can occur in either direction and does not require a universal leverage ratio or loss threshold. Actual liquidation terms depend on the instrument, collateral, mark-price method, maintenance tiers and venue procedures. A price wick alone does not measure the amount liquidated or identify its cause.
TradeHQ does not provide leveraged positions or a liquidation engine; examples remain separate arithmetic exercises.
Key points
Feedback depends on leverage, collateral rules and available liquidity
Forced reductions can amplify an adverse move; totals require event-specific evidence
Candle wicks alone cannot establish whether a cascade occurred
Why it matters when you are learning
Compare a hypothetical price shock with documented margin rules. A cascade label does not establish exact liquidation levels. TradeHQ does not implement leveraged positions or margin calls.
Worked exercise and its limits

A hypothetical $1,000 collateral amount supports $10,000 exposure. A 5% adverse price change creates a $500 loss before costs. Actual liquidation depends on maintenance requirements and venue rules; TradeHQ does not simulate forced liquidation.

Fibonacci Retracement — Trading Wiki

Fibonacci retracement plots conventional fractions of a selected price swing, often 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8% and 78.6%. The 50% level is a common chart convention, not a Fibonacci ratio, and none of these lines guarantees support or resistance.

A retracement drawing selects a price high and low, then marks fractions of their difference. Common chart conventions include 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8% and 78.6%; 50% is a midpoint convention rather than a Fibonacci-sequence ratio. The chosen endpoints and interval materially change the levels. Arithmetic does not establish that buyers or sellers will appear at a marked price. The background reference explains historical chart analysis, not a measured success rate for these ratios.

61.8% is a selected reference ratio, not a probability of a reversal
Combining chart tools does not establish a success probability

Calculate the levels from a clearly identified high and low, then compare how changing those anchors changes the chart. A Fibonacci ratio alone does not establish a reversal probability.

RSI divergence describes a mismatch between selected price swings and RSI swings.
RSI Divergence — Trading Wiki
RSI divergence describes a mismatch between selected price swings and RSI swings. It can be followed by continuation or reversal, so it is not a dependable forecast by itself.
Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. Limited source check: 2026-11-01. Checked Fidelity's RSI scale and divergence explanation and the stipulated $100/$95 and RSI 25/32 comparison. These are input values, not calculated RSI; no predictive performance, historical backtest or TradeHQ indicator equivalence was verified. This is not independent professional review.
In depth

Standard RSI compares smoothed upward and downward price changes over a selected lookback and expresses their relative strength on a 0–100 scale. A divergence compares its selected swings with price swings: for example, a lower price low alongside a higher RSI low. Those observations can occur before either a reversal or continued decline. Changing the interval or which swings count changes the comparison. No timeframe is established here as reliably predictive. Use matching external price and standard RSI data for the worksheet; the RSI-style value in TradeHQ is not a standard historical RSI calculation.
Key points
Bullish divergence: price lower low + RSI higher low
Bearish divergence: price higher high + RSI lower high
Results depend on the sample and settings; no reliable timeframe is established here
Why it matters when you are learning
Compare the price swings and RSI swings over the same dates and settings. Record both divergences followed by reversals and those followed by continuation; divergence is not an entry guarantee.
Worked exercise and its limits

Invent two observations from one matching interval: at A, price is $100 and standard RSI is 25; at B, price is $95 and RSI is 32. Price makes a lower low while RSI makes a higher low, so these stipulated swings show bullish divergence. The RSI values are given inputs, not values calculated from just these two prices. Extend the price path once to $105 and separately to $85: the same divergence can precede either outcome. TradeHQ’s RSI-style display is not a standard historical RSI series.

The MACD histogram represents the difference between the MACD line and signal line as vertical bars.
MACD Histogram — Trading Wiki
The MACD histogram represents the difference between the MACD line and signal line as vertical bars. It is calculated from past prices.
Publisher and editorial transparency
Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.
In depth

The MACD histogram is MACD minus its signal line. Under common defaults, MACD is a 12-period exponential average minus a 26-period average; the signal is a 9-period exponential average of MACD. A positive histogram means MACD exceeds the signal. Bars becoming less negative mean that difference is narrowing, not that the asset must rise. The histogram can change because either component changes. Interval, initialization and price data affect the calculation. TradeHQ does not display a MACD overlay, so calculate this example separately rather than treating the practice chart as indicator evidence.
Key points
Measures the gap between MACD line and signal line
Bars show MACD minus its signal line; a larger difference does not by itself measure price acceleration
Histogram divergence describes historical observations, not a reversal forecast
Why it matters when you are learning
Reproduce the difference between a MACD line and its signal line before interpreting the bars. This describes calculated observations, not a reliable entry or exit time.
Worked exercise and its limits

Hypothetical MACD = 2.0 and signal = 1.5 give a histogram of 0.5. If MACD stays 2.0 and the signal rises to 1.8, the histogram shrinks to 0.2 without MACD becoming negative. TradeHQ has no MACD overlay.

Bollinger Band Squeeze — Trading Wiki

A Bollinger Band squeeze describes a narrow distance between the bands relative to a selected comparison period. It reflects lower measured volatility, without specifying the direction or size of the next move.
Publisher and editorial transparency
Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.
In depth

Bollinger Bands place upper and lower bands around a moving average using a selected measure of price dispersion. A commonly used setup is a 20-period simple average with bands two standard deviations away, but settings vary. A squeeze describes relatively narrow bands compared with a stated lookback. It does not establish when volatility will increase, which direction price will move or how far. Past price distributions need not be normal, and the bands are not a guaranteed probability interval. Record the calculation and comparison period before evaluating later candles; avoid choosing a squeeze only after seeing a large move.
Key points
Narrow bands describe lower recent volatility; they do not establish when a breakout will occur
A break outside a band is an observation that can continue or reverse
Volume provides another observation, without validating a future move
Why it matters when you are learning
Compare the bandwidth over a stated sample. Narrow bands describe recent price dispersion, without storing physical energy or identifying the next move’s size or direction.
Worked exercise and its limits

Compare band widths calculated over the same interval and settings on a separate dataset. Label the narrow period before inspecting what followed. Draw both upward and downward outcomes; narrow bands do not supply a direction or deadline.

Head and Shoulders — Explanation & Learning Exercise | TradeHQ Wiki
A head and shoulders pattern has three peaks, with a higher central peak and two lower shoulders.
Head and Shoulders — Trading Wiki

A head and shoulders pattern has three peaks, with a higher central peak and two lower shoulders. A neckline connects the intervening lows; breaking it is a chart observation, not a confirmed future decline or guaranteed target.
Publisher and editorial transparency
Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.
In depth

The head and shoulders pattern is a commonly described reversal formation in technical analysis. It consists of three distinct peaks: a left shoulder, a higher central peak (the head), and a right shoulder that is approximately equal in height to the left shoulder. The troughs between these peaks are connected by a line called the neckline, and a break below this neckline completes the conventional pattern description; continued decline is a hypothesis that can fail. The conventional description follows five price phases; these observations do not establish participant motives.

Phase one: the market trends upward and creates the left shoulder, a normal swing high. Phase two: a pullback creates the first neckline touch. Phase three: renewed buying pushes price to a higher high (the head), recording a higher observed peak, without establishing acceleration or future direction. Phase four: another pullback returns to the neckline area, and bulls attempt one more push higher. Phase five: the rally fails to reach the head's height, forming the right shoulder — a lower peak that some analysts interpret as weakening upward momentum.

The measured move technique provides a price target: measure the vertical distance from the head to the neckline, then subtract that distance from the neckline breakout point. Volume adds a separate historical observation; it does not validate a forecast. Some descriptions compare volume across the shoulders, head and neckline break. State the observation window and volume source; a lower volume does not by itself establish participants’ conviction or predict the next move. Volume alone does not establish the probability that a neckline break will persist.
The inverse pattern uses three troughs rather than peaks and is commonly interpreted as a bullish hypothesis, which can fail.
Key points
Three peaks: left shoulder, head (highest), right shoulder
A neckline break describes the chart; a measured target is a projection, not a guaranteed outcome
The inverse shape can occur without a lasting upward reversal
Why it matters when you are learning
Draw the three peaks and neckline, then distinguish the pattern's measured-move convention from the actual later price. A projected target is a hypothesis rather than an expected payout.
Worked exercise and its limits

Mark three hypothetical peaks at $50, $55 and $51 with intervening lows near $46. If you project the $9 head-to-neckline height below $46, the arithmetic target is $37. It is a projection that price need not reach.

Double Bottom — Trading Wiki
A double bottom is a W-shaped chart pattern with two troughs near a similar level. A later move above the intervening peak fits the pattern, but does not ensure that a rally continues.
Publisher and editorial transparency
Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.
In depth

The double bottom is a bullish reversal pattern that forms after a sustained downtrend, characterized by two consecutive troughs at approximately the same price level separated by a moderate peak (the neckline). The pattern resembles the letter 'W' on a chart and is commonly interpreted as a possible reversal near a repeated price low; the chart alone cannot establish that selling pressure has been exhausted. The conventional description records a sequence of price observations. The first bottom forms as the existing downtrend reaches a point where buyers emerge, creating a bounce.

The subsequent rally creates the neckline — the intermediate peak between the two bottoms. However, the rally loses momentum and price declines again to retest the support level established by the first bottom. The second bottom is the critical test: if price rises again from the low, it records another bounce at that level without proving the cause or durability. In the conventional chart description, a later move above the intervening peak completes the pattern; it does not confirm a lasting reversal. The measured move target equals the depth of the pattern — the distance from the bottoms to the neckline — projected upward from the neckline breakout point.

Volume characteristics provide context but do not establish predictive reliability. Some descriptions compare volume during the two declines and the neckline break. Lower reported volume is an observation, not proof of reduced selling conviction or a future rebound. A volume observation does not establish a measured breakout failure rate. RSI divergence is another description of the selected historical data, not evidence of a dramatically higher success rate. If the RSI makes a higher low while price makes an equal or lower low at the second bottom, the oscillator records a smaller decline in its selected inputs; this does not validate a subsequent reversal.
Key points
W-shaped pattern with two tests of the same support level
A later move above the middle peak completes the conventional description, not a confirmed forecast
RSI divergence is another historical observation, not independent proof of a profitable reversal
Why it matters when you are learning
Identify the two lows and the intervening high under fixed rules, including failed examples. A familiar pattern does not establish a beginner’s readiness or confidence level.
Worked exercise and its limits

Draw troughs near $30 separated by a $35 high. The $5 height gives a conventional projection of $40 after a break above $35, but the next move could reverse. State the tolerance used to call the troughs similar.

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.
In depth

Stop loss hunting is a term used for a suspected intentional move through levels where stop orders may be placed. A chart showing a move through such a level does not establish manipulation, the identity of a trader or actual order locations. Distinguish a suspected explanation from observable prices, actual order records and findings by a market authority; similar chart movements can have different causes. In a hypothetical example, several participants could choose exits below a recent low. If the market trades through those levels, triggered sell orders could add to selling pressure.

That example describes a possible order-flow mechanism, rather than evidence that actual orders were concentrated there or that another participant deliberately moved the price. A later reversal could reflect new orders, changing liquidity, news or other causes. A wick records an interval's price range; it is not a visual signature proving a completed hunt. Public order books show displayed orders, while stop instructions, hidden orders and positions may not be publicly visible. Liquidation estimates and third-party heatmaps also require a clearly identified data source and methodology; they do not reveal every account or the location of the next price move.

Charts aggregate trades over a chosen interval, so changing the interval can change how an apparent sweep looks. To examine a suspected event, first record the instrument, venue, observation time, price and volume data. Separate that record from assumptions about hidden orders or participant intent. Compare other plausible explanations and avoid treating a single chart pattern as proof. Trading safeguards involve trade-offs. A stop-market instruction can execute at a different price from its trigger, a stop-limit instruction can remain unfilled, and an unsubmitted mental exit is not an exchange order.

Changing a stop level or using a time-based exit cannot guarantee protection against loss or an adverse move. TradeHQ's simulator currently supports market practice orders rather than automated stops. Its displayed practice charts should not be treated as forensic evidence about actual exchange manipulation.
Key points
Describes a suspected mechanism, rather than proving actual stop locations
A reversal after a level breaks does not establish deliberate manipulation
No stop buffer or exit method guarantees protection against loss
Why it matters when you are learning

A stop can be triggered before price reverses for many ordinary reasons, including volatility, clustered order flow, spread changes, and the level you chose. Avoid assuming manipulation without evidence; review the market structure and your placement instead.
