Learn how RSI Mean-Reversion works, then practise it with $100,000 virtual cash.
RSI Mean-Reversion
A step-by-step walkthrough of RSI Mean-Reversion with practice on the free $100,000 simulator.
What it is
A conceptual comparison of RSI thresholds and later price observations.

RSI compares smoothed recent gains and losses over a selected lookback and scales the result between zero and 100. Fourteen periods is a common setting; the interval must also be stated. Conventional threshold labels describe the calculation. They do not establish that an asset is mispriced or that a price reversal must follow.
Market conditions that matter

RSI can remain extreme during a sustained move or cross its thresholds repeatedly. Comparing samples labeled trending and ranging requires a rule for those labels that does not use future information. A second indicator shares price inputs and is not necessarily independent confirmation.
Study context
Studying how the same oscillator threshold behaves in different historical samples.
Limitations
An extreme reading can persist. Neither a threshold nor a second chart pattern proves a reversal.
The steps
Specify a standard RSI calculation and interval using a source that supplies the necessary historical prices.
Mark the conventional 30 and 70 thresholds as descriptions, then record all observations meeting them.
Compare later continuation and reversal cases under the same sampling and cost assumptions.
Treat entry and exit choices as separate hypothetical rules. TradeHQ’s RSI-style practice value is not a standard historical RSI calculation.
Worked example

In a fictional price dataset, an oscillator crosses a selected descriptive threshold. Compare a later continuation and a later reversal. Neither the reading nor a candlestick label establishes a price prediction or an instruction to transact.
The numbers behind it

Hypothetical comparison: fixed realized 57% wins at 1.2R and 43% losses at 1R give 0.254R gross expectancy. Changing only the assumed win rate to 32% gives 0.32×1.2−0.68=−0.296R. These chosen inputs do not establish the observed profitability of ranging or trending markets; costs and actual fills must also be considered.
How it fails
Treating an oscillator threshold as a mandatory buy or sell instruction.
Assuming a candlestick pattern proves a reversal or that simulated volume validates it.
Selecting lookbacks after seeing profitable historical outcomes without testing a separate sample.
Scope and source limitations
RSI-based results can vary sharply by market regime and rule set. Test the same rules in ranging and trending periods rather than relying on a fixed win-rate claim.

MACD Crossover
A step-by-step walkthrough of MACD Crossover with practice on the free $100,000 simulator.
What it is
A conceptual study of historical indicator crossings and their limitations.

MACD subtracts a 26-period exponential moving average from a 12-period average and compares the result with a 9-period signal line. These historical inputs create lag. A crossover can persist or reverse; the calculation does not establish a win rate, profitability or how many false starts a rule filters.
Market conditions that matter

A sustained historical move and a sideways sample can produce different numbers of crossovers. That observation does not prove a universally favorable asset class or timeframe. A filter based on a longer average is another rule to test with the same data and costs, rather than an established improvement. For a concrete comparison, label a five-bar sequence of hypothetical MACD values and identify exactly which bar produces a crossover rather than drawing a line after seeing the outcome. Record whether the signal was calculated at bar close or while the bar was still forming; that difference can alter whether a crossing appears at all. When calculated from closing prices alone, the indicator does not directly incorporate bid-ask spreads, execution priority or transaction fees.
Study context
Studying differences between moving averages, signal-line crossings and alternative exit assumptions.
Limitations
Lag and repeated crossings can create unfavorable hypothetical outcomes; no market regime guarantees performance.
The steps
Specify the price series, interval and EMA calculation; 12, 26 and 9 are conventional settings, not validated defaults.
Record each selected signal-line crossing without discarding later unfavorable cases.
Choose fictional entry and exit assumptions before calculating results, including a case where price moves before entry.
Compare costs and alternative rules in a worksheet. TradeHQ does not provide a MACD overlay or genuine short selling.
Worked example

In a fictional indicator sequence, mark a crossing and compare two alternative subsequent price paths. A selected favorable path is not an observed return, an execution guarantee or a rule for an actual order.
The numbers behind it

Hypothetical arithmetic: fixed realized 43% wins at 2.5R and 57% losses at 1R give 0.505R gross expectancy before costs. A planned reward-to-risk ratio is not the realized payoff. Losing-run probabilities depend on sample length, independence and the assumed win rate; a six-to-eight-loss run is not a universally expected outcome.
How it fails
Reporting only favorable crossings while excluding costly reversals.
Treating a planned reward-to-risk ratio as a realized payoff.
Assuming histogram divergence establishes a reversal or a profitable trade.
Scope and source limitations
MACD results vary by timeframe, market and exit rule. A selected sample's payoff distribution and drawdown describe those assumptions, not expected future performance.

Named strategy walkthroughs

The directory compares six different educational topics. Short-horizon methods, multi-day methods, indicator exercises and fixed-schedule purchases serve different questions. Examples use hypothetical inputs, not documented live performance. Read each method's limitations and supporting references before interpreting a calculation.
Strategies covered
Scalping — A short-horizon price and transaction-cost comparison; no fixed interval defines the concept.
Swing Trading — A comparison of multi-session price observations and overnight exposure.
Day Trading — Opening and closing all positions within a single session.
Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA) — Investing equal amounts on a predetermined schedule rather than selecting each purchase date based on a price prediction.
RSI Mean-Reversion — A conceptual comparison of RSI thresholds and later price observations.

A simple comparison before choosing a worksheet

Consider two different teaching questions: a fixed $100 contribution made at three specified dates is a cash-flow exercise, whereas recording a MACD crossing on three observations is an indicator-definition exercise. They do not use the same denominator or imply comparable expected returns. For the contribution exercise, list total cash added and total units; for an indicator exercise, state the source, price interval and calculation before counting any signals.

Neither example needs a live trade. The choice of an exercise should follow the concept being studied, not a claim that a holding period or indicator offers a better outcome. Any comparison of observed results needs consistent date ranges, costs, valuation conventions and a clear statement that a selected sample cannot verify future performance.
What a strategy is, and what it is not

A trading rule describes a testable set of conditions and assumptions. Dollar-cost averaging is different: it schedules contributions, without requiring an active entry or exit signal. The site presents these methods for comparison, not as advice about which method is suitable for a person.

A chosen win percentage without the payoff distribution and costs is not enough to evaluate outcomes. Results from a selected historical or virtual sample are descriptive; they may change in another sample. No source-backed universal winning percentage or account-return forecast is offered.
Testing a strategy without fooling yourself
Write down the hypothetical assumptions and observation window before reviewing outcomes.
Avoid treating 30, 100 or any other arbitrary number of observations as a universal statistical threshold. Sample design, selection and dependence matter.
Record cases selected by the exercise criteria, including unfavorable cases and changes to the rule.
If using sample expectancy or drawdown, explicitly label the costs, sizes, dates and limitations of the input data.
Check the effect of a negative-outcome sequence without asserting how often it will occur in practice.
Compare a second specified sample without claiming that a backtest establishes future results.

What Is an Option? Calls & Puts Explained

A stock option gives its buyer a contractual right; contract size, exercise style and settlement terms determine what that right involves. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
A stock option gives its buyer a contractual right; contract size, exercise style and settlement terms determine what that right involves.
The core definition

This lesson focuses on standard unadjusted US equity options, which generally cover 100 shares. A call gives its buyer a right to buy and a put a right to sell at the strike under the contract terms. American-style options can be exercised before expiry; European-style options have a different exercise schedule. Adjusted contracts and cash-settled index options can have different deliverables. The writer takes the corresponding obligation. Read the specific contract and OCC risk disclosure rather than assume every option is identical.

For a standard unadjusted 100-share contract, the quoted premium is stated per share. An option premium depends on multiple pricing inputs, including the underlying price, strike, remaining time, implied volatility, interest rates and dividends. It is not a direct measure of an individual participant's expectations.
Why options exist

A share holder can buy a put to offset some losses below its strike during the option term, at the cost of its premium. A covered call adds premium income but limits upside and retains substantial share-price risk. These examples illustrate different payoffs; neither is a guaranteed return or a universally suitable position.
A simple worked example

Imagine Apple trades at $180 and you buy one 30-day $185 call for $3.00 ($300 total). Three things can happen. If Apple closes above $188 on expiration, you're profitable — the intrinsic value of the call exceeds what you paid. An expiration price strictly between $185 and $188 gives the call intrinsic value but a net loss before costs; $188 is gross break-even. If it closes at or below $185, the call expires worthless and you lose the full $300 — but nothing more. These are hypothetical expiration payoffs before costs for the purchased option alone. Exercise can create a stock position with separate funding and market risk. Short options have different obligations, and an uncovered short call can have unlimited loss.
What you can practise on TradeHQ

TradeHQ supports spot instruments, including shares and ETFs, with $100,000 virtual capital. It does not model option strikes, expirations or premiums. Use this lesson's worked examples to calculate hypothetical contract payoffs on paper; buying an underlying share in the simulator is a different transaction from buying an option on it.
> Options are contracts, not shares. Time value generally erodes as expiry approaches, but the total premium can rise or fall with other pricing inputs.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)
Key takeaways
A standard unadjusted US equity option generally covers 100 shares; adjusted and other contracts can differ.
At expiration, before costs, a purchased call has a net gain above strike + premium; a purchased put has a net gain below strike − premium. Those levels are break-even prices.
A purchased option held without exercise can lose its premium plus costs; exercise can create a separate underlying position and obligations.
Options can be used for hedging and speculation; their risk depends on the position and contract.

How many shares does one standard US equity option contract control? Options: 10; 50; 100; 1,000. Correct answer: 100. Why: A standard unadjusted US equity option generally covers 100 shares. Adjusted deliverables and other option types differ.

What is the maximum loss for someone who buys (goes long) a single call option? Options: Unlimited; The strike price × 100; The premium paid; The stock price × 100. Correct answer: The premium paid. Why: For the purchased option alone before exercise and costs, loss is limited to the premium. Exercise can create a separate position.

A call option gives the buyer the right to: Options: Sell shares at the strike price; Buy shares at the strike price; Short the stock; Receive dividends. Correct answer: Buy shares at the strike price. Why: Call = right to buy. Put = right to sell.

Buying a protective put alongside shares is an example of: Options: Eliminating every cost; A guaranteed gain; Hedging downside exposure; Avoiding contract terms. Correct answer: Hedging downside exposure. Why: A put can offset some downside below its strike, but the premium, expiry and other terms matter.

The Greeks — Delta, Gamma, Theta & Vega

These four Greeks describe model-based sensitivities to underlying prices, time and implied volatility; they do not guarantee realized price changes. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
These four Greeks describe model-based sensitivities to underlying prices, time and implied volatility; they do not guarantee realized price changes.
Why Greeks matter

Greeks are model-based sensitivities to inputs, holding other inputs fixed. Delta describes underlying-price sensitivity; gamma describes a change in delta; theta describes time sensitivity; vega describes implied-volatility sensitivity. Interest rates and dividends can also matter. Finite market moves need not equal a first-order estimate, and different pricing models can produce different values.
Delta — directional exposure

A delta of 0.50 per share describes an approximate $0.50 option-price change for a $1 underlying move, with other inputs held fixed. For a 100-share contract that is about $50, before gamma and other effects. Some traders use delta as a rough probability shorthand, but it is not a calibrated real-world probability and need not match the model probability of finishing in the money.
Gamma — how fast delta changes

Gamma measures how delta changes as the underlying moves. It is often relatively large near the strike close to expiry, depending on volatility and other inputs. Dealer hedging can affect demand, but a chart or open-interest figure alone does not establish dealer positions, required hedges or the cause of a price move.
Theta — the ticking clock

Theta estimates an option value change as time passes under a model, holding other inputs fixed. State whether the quote is per share or per contract and whether a calendar or trading-day convention is used. Purchased options commonly have negative theta, but realised profit also depends on price, volatility and costs. Selling premium is not a guaranteed collection of that estimate.
Vega — volatility sensitivity

Vega estimates sensitivity to a one-percentage-point change in implied volatility, with other inputs held fixed. Implied volatility can change around earnings, but it need not rise before every release or fall afterwards. A long option can lose despite a favorable underlying move if time decay and a volatility decline offset that move.

> Options have several model sensitivities: delta describes underlying-price sensitivity, gamma describes how delta changes with the underlying price, and theta and vega describe time and volatility sensitivities. Hold other model inputs fixed when interpreting each measure.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)
Key takeaways
Delta estimates underlying-price sensitivity, not a guaranteed payoff or real-world event probability.
Gamma is often relatively large near the strike close to expiration; volatility and other model inputs also matter.
Theta is a model sensitivity; other price changes can offset or exceed it.
Vega measures volatility sensitivity; a change in implied volatility is a different quantity.
Check your understanding

What does theta measure? Options: Directional exposure; Time decay per day; Volatility sensitivity; Interest-rate risk. Correct answer: Time decay per day. Why: Theta is a model estimate of time sensitivity with other inputs held fixed; units and time conventions must be stated.

In the lesson example, a 0.50 delta and a $1 underlying rise imply approximately what change per option share, before other effects? Options: $0.10; $0.30; $0.50; $0.90. Correct answer: $0.50. Why: 0.50 × $1 = $0.50 per share, holding other inputs fixed; this is not an event probability.

Which event can be followed by a sharp decline in implied volatility? Options: A fixed time every morning; An earnings announcement resolving uncertainty; Every market opening without exception; Every dividend payment without exception. Correct answer: An earnings announcement resolving uncertainty. Why: A sharp post-announcement decline in implied volatility is sometimes called IV crush. It is not confined to earnings and is not inevitable after an announcement.
Which Greek measures the rate of change of delta? Options: Vega; Theta; Gamma; Rho. Correct answer: Gamma. Why: Gamma tells you how quickly delta itself changes.

Defined-Risk Spreads — Verticals & Iron Condors

Vertical spreads and iron condors illustrate bounded expiration payoffs, with execution and assignment risks to consider. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
Vertical spreads and iron condors illustrate bounded expiration payoffs, with execution and assignment risks to consider.
Comparing expiration payoffs

A spread combines long and short options. Certain vertical spreads have bounded theoretical payoffs at expiration, unlike an uncovered short call. That comparison does not make spreads universally safe or suitable for beginners. TradeHQ does not execute options spreads; the examples below are worksheet exercises.
Bull call spread — a hypothetical example

Assume one standard 100-share contract per leg, the same expiration, a $180 long call costing $4 per share and a $185 short call receiving $2. The net debit is $200. With both legs resolved as the expiration payoff assumes, the maximum loss is $200 and the maximum gain is ($185 - $180) × 100 - $200 = $300, before costs. At a $182 expiration price, the $200 intrinsic value offsets the debit for gross break-even. These selected quotes are arithmetic inputs, not current Apple prices or a recommended trade.
Iron condor — another payoff structure

A short iron condor combines a put credit spread below and a call credit spread above the underlying price. With all four legs intact, its expiration payoff has a maximum gain equal to the net credit when the price lies between the short strikes. Movement beyond the range can produce a loss. Time decay and implied volatility affect its value before expiration; this structure is an example for comparison rather than a preferred trade.
A hypothetical sizing worksheet

For arithmetic practice, suppose a worksheet assigns 1-2% of a hypothetical $100,000 account to a trade's planned loss budget: that is $1,000-$2,000. These percentages are assumptions, not an institutional standard or a recommendation for a real account. Repeated losses reduce equity, and correlated positions can lose together. The percentage alone does not establish how many trades an account can withstand.
What the payoff diagram leaves out

Costs and poor fills can change realised results. American-style short options can be assigned before expiration. Exercise or assignment of only one leg can leave stock exposure, particularly near a strike at expiration. A bounded payoff diagram assumes the legs are maintained and resolved together; it is not a guarantee about every account outcome. Closing a spread can reduce remaining expiration exposure but adds execution costs and cannot undo earlier assignment.
Worksheet comparison

Calculate the bull call example at expiration prices of $175, $182 and $190. Then add an assumed $8 in total costs: the gross outcomes of -$200, $0 and +$300 become -$208, -$8 and +$292. Separately describe what could happen if the short leg were assigned and the stock position remained open. Keep that exposure separate from the intact-spread payoff.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)
Key takeaways
Certain spreads have bounded theoretical expiration payoffs when their legs remain intact.
The example's $200 debit and $300 maximum gain exclude costs and additional stock exposure.
An iron condor's range-based payoff does not make it a preferred or safe trade.
TradeHQ supports spot simulation; options spreads are studied in worksheets.
Check your understanding

For the intact bull call example, maximum expiration loss before costs is: Options: Unlimited; The width of the spread; The $200 net debit; The strike price. Correct answer: The $200 net debit. Why: Both calls expire worthless below $180, leaving the $200 debit as the gross loss. Costs and separate stock exposure are excluded.

An intact short iron condor has its maximum gross expiration gain when the underlying: Options: Rallies sharply beyond the upper wing; Crashes beyond the lower wing; Finishes between the short strikes; Goes to zero. Correct answer: Finishes between the short strikes. Why: The four options expire without intrinsic value between the short strikes, leaving the credit before costs.

In the worksheet, 1-2% of a hypothetical $100,000 account equals: Options: $50,000; $25,000; $1,000-$2,000; $100. Correct answer: $1,000-$2,000. Why: 100,000 × 0.01 to 0.02 = $1,000-$2,000. The percentages are illustrative assumptions, not a universal standard.

Why can an expiration payoff diagram understate account exposure? Options: It guarantees a profit; It includes all commissions; Assignment of one leg can leave a stock position; Spreads cannot lose. Correct answer: Assignment of one leg can leave a stock position. Why: The intact-spread payoff assumes both legs are resolved together. Assignment can create separate stock exposure and costs.

Implied Volatility & Trading Around Earnings

Implied volatility is a model-implied input derived from option prices, with limits as a forecast of realised volatility. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
Implied volatility is a model-implied input derived from option prices, with limits as a forecast of realised volatility.
What implied volatility actually is

Implied volatility (IV) is the volatility figure that, plugged into an option pricing model, would produce the option's current market price. It is not a prediction any single person makes — it emerges from the aggregate bids and offers of every participant. Changes can reflect expected uncertainty, demand for protection and risk premiums. IV is model-dependent and need not equal later realised volatility.
IV rank vs IV percentile

A quoted IV value needs context before comparisons can be interpreted. IV rank commonly compares current IV with the highest and lowest observations over a specified lookback, often 52 weeks, on a 0–100 scale. A constant series has no high-low range, so the usual calculation is undefined. Under one common convention, IV percentile is the fraction of observations below the current value over a stated lookback. Check the provider's treatment of equal observations and the chosen series. Neither an IV-rank threshold nor an IV-percentile threshold establishes a buy or sell rule. Compare the chosen lookback, option expiry, price source and costs before interpreting either measure.
The earnings trap

Implied volatility often rises before earnings and can fall sharply afterwards. A trader can be directionally correct and still lose on a long option if the volatility drop and time decay outweigh the price move.
Comparing hypothetical earnings payoffs

In a paper worksheet, compare hypothetical long-premium and defined-risk premium-selling structures around earnings to see how direction, implied volatility and the size of the actual move interact. TradeHQ does not price these structures. Avoid treating volatility selling as inherently safer; short premium can carry substantial risk.
Practice loop

For a historical study, record dated option quotes and implied-volatility observations from an options-data source before and after an earnings announcement. Keep the expiry, strike and data methodology consistent, and record price changes as well as volatility changes. TradeHQ does not supply an options chain or IV-rank data. A small sample can illustrate mechanisms without establishing a reliable trading edge.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)
Key takeaways
IV is inferred from option prices under a model; it can differ from future realised volatility.
IV rank contextualises today's IV against the last 12 months.
IV crush after earnings can turn a correct directional bet into a loss.
Elevated implied volatility changes the payoff profile of premium-selling strategies, but higher premiums also reflect higher expected uncertainty and risk.
Check your understanding

Under the lesson's 52-week high-low convention, what does IV rank of 80 describe? Options: IV is at 80%; IV is toward the upper end of its observed range; IV is near a 12-month low; 80% of options are profitable. Correct answer: IV is toward the upper end of its observed range. Why: IV rank describes relative location within a specified high-low range, not the fraction of days below the current value.

Why can a long option lose even if the price moves in the expected direction after earnings? Options: Because options never follow the underlying; A drop in implied volatility and time value can offset the directional gain; Because earnings cancel the contract; Because all options are illiquid. Correct answer: A drop in implied volatility and time value can offset the directional gain. Why: Option value depends on more than direction; implied volatility and time value can change sharply after earnings.

What does a high IV rank tell you? Options: A premium-selling trade is guaranteed to work; Current implied volatility is high relative to its own recent range; The stock must fall; The next move will be small. Correct answer: Current implied volatility is high relative to its own recent range. Why: IV rank is context about relative option pricing, not a standalone buy or sell signal.

Implied volatility is: Options: Historical vol over 30 days; An exchange forecast; The volatility that makes model = market price; The stock's beta. Correct answer: The volatility that makes model = market price. Why: IV is the vol input that reconciles a pricing model with the live option price.

The worksheet uses a hypothetical loss assumption for arithmetic comparison; it does not require entering any position. For example, 1% of a $100,000 practice account is $1,000. This is an educational parameter, not a universal real-money rule.
Testing a hypothetical loss multiplier

Naked puts and short strangles can create losses far larger than the premium collected. In a paper worksheet, model adverse moves explicitly and compare the resulting losses with a hypothetical risk budget rather than relying on one fixed multiplier. TradeHQ does not execute these option positions.
Rolling — definition and limitations

Rolling means closing an existing option and opening another with a different expiry and sometimes a different strike. A credit or debit alone does not determine whether the adjustment makes sense; compare the new maximum loss, break-even points, time remaining and total capital at risk in a worked example. Rolling options is not supported by TradeHQ's order engine.
When to cut a loss

Predefined exits can prevent open-ended decision-making, but no single percentage works for every option structure. In a worksheet with appropriate historical option prices, compare several hypothetical exit rules and record drawdown, average loss and opportunity cost. Account for execution assumptions and costs; TradeHQ's spot simulator cannot perform this options backtest.
Journaling every trade

For each hypothetical options example, record the thesis, dated volatility inputs, contract size, possible loss, exit assumptions and calculated P&L in a separate worksheet. What Is a Futures Contract?

A futures contract is a standardised, exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell a fixed quantity of an asset at a set price on a set future date. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
A futures contract is a standardised, exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell a fixed quantity of an asset at a set price on a set future date.
The core definition

A futures contract is a standardised, exchange-traded agreement with a specified underlying asset or reference, contract size and settlement date. Settlement can involve physical delivery or a cash payment under the contract rules. The clearing house acts as central counterparty to cleared trades and uses margin, settlement and default safeguards to manage risk. Clearing reduces counterparty exposure; it does not make default impossible or protect a position from market losses.
Contract specifications matter

Every futures contract has a spec sheet: contract size, tick size, tick value, trading hours, delivery month, and settlement method (physical or cash). These details determine the exposure and settlement obligations. One E-mini S&P 500 contract represents $50 × the index — with the index at 5,000, a single contract has $250,000 of notional exposure.
Long and short positions

A participant can open a long futures position by buying or a short position by selling the contract. A short futures position does not require first borrowing the underlying asset as a short stock sale does. Both directions remain subject to margin requirements, broker permissions and applicable exchange rules, including position limits. The contract's settlement obligations still matter; being able to sell first does not mean that trading is unrestricted.
Speculators and price discovery

Hedgers use futures to offset exposure to price changes in another activity or holding. Speculators accept price exposure in pursuit of a trading profit. For a hypothetical producer, a short futures position may offset some losses from a falling sale price; the hedge can be imperfect if the cash and futures prices move differently. These roles help explain why participants trade. This lesson does not assign a universal percentage of market volume to either group.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)
Key takeaways
A futures contract is a standardised exchange agreement with a specified underlying or reference and settlement terms.
The clearing house manages counterparty risk through safeguards; it does not eliminate all risk.
Both long and short futures positions remain subject to margin, permissions and exchange rules.
Every contract has a spec sheet — always read it.

This is an example of: Options: Guaranteed profit; Eliminating default risk; Hedging price exposure; Avoiding all settlement obligations. Correct answer: Hedging price exposure. Margin & Leverage in Futures

Futures margin is collateral for contract obligations. Losses and variation-margin demands can exceed an initial margin deposit. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
Futures margin is collateral for contract obligations. Losses and variation-margin demands can exceed an initial margin deposit.
Margin is not what you think

Stock margin can involve borrowing to purchase shares. Futures margin is collateral, often called a performance bond, rather than a loan to purchase the contract's notional value. It does not cap losses. Exchange requirements vary by contract and market conditions, and brokers can require additional funds. The figures below are a hypothetical worksheet, not current margin requirements.
Maintenance margin and margin calls

Maintenance margin is the minimum account equity required to maintain a position. It is not a universal percentage of initial margin. A shortfall can require additional funds or a reduction in positions; a broker may liquidate positions under its rules. Requirements can change, and action may occur intraday. Check the contract requirements and broker agreement instead of assuming a fixed deadline or a guaranteed warning.
Daily mark-to-market

Futures positions are marked to market, with gains and losses settled through variation margin. Daily settlement limits the accumulation of unpaid losses, and clearing arrangements may include intraday settlement. It does not eliminate default or overnight risk: clearing houses also use collateral and other financial safeguards. A hypothetical $2,000 loss reduces the account's funds; the timing of customer-account entries depends on the broker's arrangements.
Why leverage cuts both ways

For a hypothetical E-mini S&P 500 contract at an index level of 5,000, the $50 multiplier gives $250,000 of notional exposure. A 1% index move is 50 points, or $2,500 per contract before costs. Relative to an assumed $13,000 margin deposit, that is about 19.2%; it is not a percentage of every trader's total account equity. A different index level, contract quantity or account balance changes the calculation.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)
Key takeaways
Futures margin is a performance bond, not a loan.
Accounts are marked-to-market every trading day.
A maintenance shortfall can require more funds, reduced positions or liquidation under broker rules.
Leverage depends on contract exposure and the equity used in the calculation.
Check your understanding

Futures margin is best described as: Options: A loan; A performance bond; A fee; A tax. Correct answer: A performance bond. Why: It is collateral supporting the position, not a loan or a cap on losses.
Futures accounts are marked-to-market: Options: Yearly; Monthly; Every trading day; Only at expiration. Correct answer: Every trading day. Why: Daily settlement moves cash in/out.
In the worksheet (index 5,000, $50 multiplier), a 1% move relative to an assumed $13,000 deposit is approximately: Options: 1%; 5%; ~19%; 50%. Correct answer: ~19%. Why: $2,500 on $13,000 ≈ 19%.

A margin call means: Options: You made money; A collateral shortfall may require funds or position reduction; Exchange closed; Broker owes interest. Correct answer: A collateral shortfall may require funds or position reduction. Why: The broker may require additional funds or reduce or liquidate positions under its rules.

Contango & Backwardation — Term Structure Explained — Futures & Derivatives | TradeHQ
Compare prices across delivery dates and study carrying costs, supply conditions and the assumptions behind rolling exposure.
Contango & Backwardation — Term Structure Explained

Compare prices across delivery dates and study carrying costs, supply conditions and the assumptions behind rolling exposure. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
Compare prices across delivery dates and study carrying costs, supply conditions and the assumptions behind rolling exposure.
Term structure — the futures curve

A futures curve compares quoted prices across the delivery dates available for a specified contract family and observation time. The number of listed expirations varies by product and exchange. Later delivery priced above nearer delivery is commonly called contango; the reverse comparison is backwardation. State which dates are being compared rather than assume the entire curve has one slope.
Why contango happens

Carrying costs such as storage, insurance and financing can contribute to higher prices for later delivery. A simplified example with $4 of carrying costs may illustrate that relationship, but convenience yield, constraints and market conditions also matter; there is no universal $4 premium or default curve.
Why backwardation happens

Backwardation means later-delivery contracts trade below nearer delivery in the comparison being made. Supply conditions and the value of immediate availability can contribute, but the curve alone does not prove a physical shortage or identify a future price direction.
The roll yield trap

A fund with futures exposure may replace expiring contracts according to its current published methodology. Rolling can affect performance relative to spot, alongside collateral returns, fees and the price path. A roll is not an automatic cash loss equal to the price gap; inspect the specific fund and observation period.
Trading implications

The curve records prices for different delivery dates. It is context for an educational comparison, not an automatic top, bottom or squeeze signal and not a direct measurement of commercial hedger positioning.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)
Key takeaways
Contango: later delivery trades above nearer delivery in the comparison; carrying costs can contribute.
Backwardation: later delivery trades below nearer delivery; the curve alone does not establish a shortage.
Futures-fund returns depend on methodology, contract price changes, collateral returns and costs.
The curve shows delivery prices, not the identity or positioning of participants.
Check your understanding

For two stated delivery months, what describes a lower price for the later delivery? Options: Contango; Backwardation; Equilibrium; Rollover. Correct answer: Backwardation. Why: Backwardation describes relative delivery prices; it does not by itself prove a shortage.

Which factor can make a futures fund differ from spot performance? Options: Guaranteed gains; Contract selection and rolling methodology; No costs; Identical exposure. Correct answer: Contract selection and rolling methodology. Why: Methodology, contract price changes, collateral returns and costs affect fund performance.

Which factor can contribute to contango in a storable-commodity example? Options: A guaranteed shortage; Carrying costs; The ticker symbol alone; A universal price rule. Correct answer: Carrying costs. Why: Carrying costs can contribute to higher deferred futures prices. Convenience yield and other conditions can offset those costs; storable commodities are not always in contango.

Which condition can contribute to backwardation, without being proven by the curve alone? Options: Quiet market; Physical shortage; Delisting; Low vol. Correct answer: Physical shortage. Why: Immediate demand for physical supply and convenience yield can contribute to backwardation. The curve alone does not prove a shortage or identify participants’ motives.

Hedging with Futures — The Original Use Case

Hedging is one use of futures. Airlines may hedge fuel, producers may hedge output, and funds may hedge equity beta. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
Hedging is one use of futures. Airlines may hedge fuel, producers may hedge output, and funds may hedge equity beta.
The airline case study

Hypothetical cross-hedge: an airline with future jet-fuel costs considers a crude-oil futures position. Rising futures prices could offset part of a higher fuel bill, but jet fuel and crude oil are different products, the hedge quantity and delivery dates may not match, and margins can require cash before the fuel purchase. It is not a lock on the airline’s complete fuel cost.
The farmer case study

Hypothetical producer hedge: a farmer expecting to sell corn later takes a short futures position in a chosen contract month. A fall in the futures price could produce a gain offsetting part of a lower cash sale price. The final result also depends on local basis, quantity, crop yield, contract terms and costs. The futures entry price is not a guarantee of the final net farm receipt.
Portfolio hedging with equity index futures

In a hypothetical worksheet, $50 million divided by $250,000 of contract notional gives 200 contracts. That arithmetic assumes one-for-one exposure; actual hedge sizing also depends on portfolio beta, basis risk and contract specifications. It does not guarantee full neutralisation or establish trading volume.
The hedge is never perfect

Basis risk concerns changes in the relationship between the hedged exposure and the futures price. A hedge can reduce one exposure while introducing margin liquidity, execution and operational risks. Its effectiveness depends on the products, quantities, dates and outcome being measured; neither complete protection nor a fixed amount of risk reduction follows from the label hedge.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)
Key takeaways
Hedging uses a position to offset a specified exposure; it need not eliminate every risk.
Hedge direction depends on the specific price exposure being offset.
A conceptual index-futures hedge can reduce some equity-market exposure; mismatch and other risks remain.
Basis changes, cash-flow needs and mismatched quantities can affect a hedge.
Check your understanding

Which conceptual futures direction offsets some exposure to a falling wheat sale price? Options: Buy wheat futures; Sell wheat futures; Buy corn futures; Buy S&P. Correct answer: Sell wheat futures. Why: A short wheat future can gain when its futures price falls, but basis, quantity and costs affect the combined result.

Which conceptual crude futures position gains if its futures price rises? Options: Sell crude futures; Buy crude futures; Buy S&P; Do nothing. Correct answer: Buy crude futures. Why: The hypothetical price exposure has a positive gross change if its referenced futures price rises. Costs and the separate fuel expense still matter.

Basis risk is: Options: Exchange default; Futures vs physical don't move perfectly together; Rate risk; FX risk. Correct answer: Futures vs physical don't move perfectly together. Why: Basis fluctuates.

In the simplified one-for-one notional worksheet, what is the count represented by $50 million divided by $250,000? Options: 20; 200; 500; 1,000. Correct answer: 200. Why: The quotient is 200 under the specified arithmetic assumption; this is not an actual hedge-size recommendation.

Micro Futures — Contract Size and Risk

Compare Micro E-mini equity-index contracts with their E-mini counterparts, while checking each product’s specifications and risks. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
Compare Micro E-mini equity-index contracts with their E-mini counterparts, while checking each product’s specifications and risks.
What micros are

CME's Micro E-mini S&P 500, Nasdaq-100, Dow and Russell 2000 contracts are one-tenth the size of their respective E-mini equity-index contracts. For example, MES has a $5 multiplier per index point, compared with $50 for ES. Do not apply that ratio to every product called micro, including unrelated crypto contracts. Margin requirements must be checked separately with the exchange and broker.
Smaller contracts still carry risk

A smaller contract allows finer adjustments to notional exposure, but does not establish a trading edge or prevent excessive risk. Ten MES contracts have the same index-point exposure as one ES contract, before differences in costs. Compare the total number of contracts, account equity and potential price movement rather than assuming that a micro label makes a position safe.
Compare the contract specifications

MES and ES both use a 0.25-index-point minimum price increment. That tick is worth $1.25 for one MES contract and $12.50 for one ES contract. Futures margin and settlement principles apply to both, but fees, liquidity and broker requirements need separate checks. For a hypothetical index level of 5,000, one MES contract represents $25,000 of notional exposure; the margin deposit is not the amount of exposure or a maximum loss.
On the simulator

TradeHQ's $100,000 practice account supports spot instruments. It does not model futures contracts, initial or maintenance margin, daily settlement, or margin calls. Use a paper worksheet to calculate a hypothetical contract's daily P&L and margin balance; buying a similarly named spot instrument does not reproduce futures mechanics.

Reading CPI and Inflation Data

CPI measures selected consumer-price changes. Read the release, its definitions and components without assuming a predictable market response. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
CPI measures selected consumer-price changes. Read the release, its definitions and components without assuming a predictable market response.
What CPI actually measures

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes CPI indexes measuring changes in consumer prices over time using sampled prices and expenditure weights. This lesson focuses on the all-urban-consumers index (CPI-U) and its all-items and all-items-less-food-and-energy measures, often called headline and core CPI. Core readings are used to study trends, while the FOMC states its longer-run 2% inflation goal in terms of the annual change in the PCE price index.
The release mechanics

Check the current BLS release calendar for CPI timing; scheduled releases are generally at 8:30 AM Eastern. Market reactions depend on expectations and other information. No fixed first-minute percentage move or single class of participant is established by this lesson.
Consensus, surprise and market reaction

A consensus figure is an aggregation of a particular survey’s forecasts, not the view of every economist. Record the provider, collection time and aggregation method before comparing it with the release. The difference is often called a surprise, but its sign alone cannot determine yields, exchange rates or share returns; expectations, revisions and other information can also matter.
The three-layer read

For a study worksheet, compare the reported headline and core changes with a specifically identified expectation, then inspect the component contributions and measurement period. Headline and core answer different questions. The Fed’s stated longer-run target uses PCE inflation rather than either CPI measure, and policy considers more than one statistic.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)
Key takeaways
Use the current BLS release calendar; releases are generally scheduled at 8:30 AM Eastern.
Core CPI excludes food and energy; the FOMC’s longer-run inflation target uses PCE.
A release-versus-survey difference is context, not a deterministic market signal.
Read the underlying components.
Check your understanding

The Fed's 2% longer-run inflation goal is measured using: Options: Headline CPI; Core CPI; PCE price index; PPI. Correct answer: PCE price index. Why: The FOMC states its 2% longer-run inflation goal in terms of the annual change in the PCE price index.

What release time is generally listed on the BLS CPI release calendar? Options: 8:00 AM ET; 8:30 AM ET; 10:00 AM ET; 2:00 PM ET. Correct answer: 8:30 AM ET. Why: The published calendar generally lists 8:30 AM Eastern. Consult the current calendar because schedules can change.

What distinguishes core CPI from headline CPI? Options: Core is always higher; Core excludes food and energy; Headline CPI is not reported; Core predicts future inflation. Correct answer: Core excludes food and energy. Why: Core CPI excludes food and energy, whose prices can be volatile. It offers one view of underlying inflation; headline CPI covers the full specified basket. Neither series alone establishes future inflation.

A CPI result above one survey’s median forecast establishes: Options: The next stock return; A difference from that specified forecast; A guaranteed rate increase; Which participant moved the market. Correct answer: A difference from that specified forecast. Why: A forecast difference alone does not identify market participants or determine the next price move.

The Fed & FOMC Cycle — How Rates Get Set

The FOMC has eight regularly scheduled meetings a year, and its decisions can affect market expectations. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
The FOMC has eight regularly scheduled meetings a year, and its decisions can affect market expectations.
The mandate

The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy under statutory goals that include maximum employment and stable prices. The FOMC states a 2% longer-run inflation goal measured by the annual change in the PCE price index and considers a wide range of economic information when making decisions.
The eight-meeting cycle

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) schedules eight regular meetings a year and can hold additional meetings when needed. In 2026, regular policy-setting meetings have been followed by a policy statement and Chair press conference, with four scheduled projection releases. The Federal Reserve's November 12, 2026 revised tentative 2027 calendar designates October 26–27 as a strategy-only meeting; a policy decision is not scheduled for that meeting. Use the current official calendar for meeting types, statements and projection dates.
Market pricing of Fed decisions

The CME FedWatch Tool converts federal-funds futures prices into implied probabilities for possible policy outcomes. Those probabilities describe market pricing, not certainty. Market reactions depend on the decision, accompanying statement, economic outlook and what participants had already expected.
Reading the statement vs the presser

The policy statement records the Committee's decision and assessment. The post-meeting press conference can add context beyond the statement and projections, so market participants may react to both the written release and the Chair's answers.
Trading the Fed

For an educational exercise, observe how prices react around the statement and press conference rather than assuming the first move is predictable. Short-term reactions can change as participants process new information.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)

The Fed pursues its statutory employment and price-stability goals; the FOMC states a 2% longer-run PCE inflation goal.
The FOMC schedules eight regular meetings a year; meeting types and projection release schedules can change. The revised tentative 2027 calendar includes a strategy-only meeting.
CME FedWatch shows futures-implied probabilities, not certain outcomes.
The press conference can add information beyond the written statement.

The 'dot plot' shows: Options: Historical rates; Each participant's assessment of appropriate policy; Balance sheet; Sentiment. Correct answer: Each participant's assessment of appropriate policy. Why: The dots record individual participants’ assessments of an appropriate policy path, not only voting members and not a Committee promise.

FedWatch derives probabilities from: Options: Analyst surveys; Fed funds futures pricing; Twitter; Reuters polls. Correct answer: Fed funds futures pricing. Why: Fed funds futures embed implied rate probabilities.

The Yield Curve and Recession-Risk Research

Yield-curve inversion has historically been associated with elevated US recession risk, but timing varies and the signal is not a standalone forecast. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
Yield-curve inversion has historically been associated with elevated US recession risk, but timing varies and the signal is not a standalone forecast.
What the yield curve is

A Treasury yield curve describes yields across maturities at a stated time. The US Treasury currently publishes daily estimated par yields for maturities from one month through thirty years. An upward-sloping curve has higher longer-term yields than shorter-term yields; a selected spread is inverted when the shorter-term yield exceeds the longer-term yield. The shape can vary over time and across maturity pairs.
Why inversion can indicate recession risk

An inverted curve can reflect expectations for slower growth, lower future policy rates, or changing term premia. Historically, commonly watched Treasury-curve inversions have often preceded US recessions, but the lead time varies and the relationship is not a deterministic forecast.
The 10Y-2Y vs 10Y-3M

The linked New York Fed research model uses the ten-year minus three-month Treasury yield spread to estimate recession probability twelve months ahead; the researchers explicitly distinguish these estimates from official Federal Reserve forecasts. The ten-year minus two-year spread is a different series. Model probabilities depend on the model and sample and are not certain outcomes; the two spreads need not invert on the same date.
Trading around the curve
The curve is a slow-moving macro indicator. Treat it as one piece of economic context rather than as an intraday timing tool or an automatic instruction to change a portfolio.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)
Key takeaways
An upward-sloping curve has higher longer-term yields than shorter-term yields; curve shapes can vary.
Inversions have historically been associated with elevated recession risk, with timing that varies across cycles.
The linked NY Fed recession model uses the ten-year minus three-month Treasury yield spread.
Use the curve as one macro indicator alongside other evidence.

Inverted curve = Options: Short < long; Short > long; Flat; Negative yields. Correct answer: Short > long. Why: Short-term exceeds long-term.

Which spread does the linked NY Fed recession model use? Options: 10Y-2Y; 10Y-3M; 30Y-5Y; 2Y-Fed Funds. Correct answer: 10Y-3M. Why: The linked New York Fed research model uses the 10-year minus 3-month Treasury spread; its estimates are not official Federal Reserve forecasts.

What is the safest interpretation of a yield-curve inversion? Options: It guarantees a recession; It is one historical recession-risk indicator with uncertain timing; It predicts the exact market bottom; It only matters for day traders. Correct answer: It is one historical recession-risk indicator with uncertain timing. Why: Yield-curve inversion is informative context, but it is not a guaranteed or precisely timed forecast.

The yield curve by itself provides: Options: An exact entry time; A dated description of yields across maturities; Guaranteed equity returns; One required asset allocation. Correct answer: A dated description of yields across maturities. Why: A curve describes relative yields; any forecast requires additional assumptions and remains uncertain.

The Dollar Index (DXY) — Reading Currency Context

DXY tracks the dollar against six currencies and offers context for studying currency exposure, with important limits. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
DXY tracks the dollar against six currencies and offers context for studying currency exposure, with important limits.
What the basket measures

ICE's US Dollar Index measures the dollar against six currencies: euro (57.6%), Japanese yen (13.6%), British pound (11.9%), Canadian dollar (9.1%), Swedish krona (4.2%) and Swiss franc (3.6%). It is heavily weighted toward the euro and excludes many trading partners. A DXY rise therefore does not imply the same dollar appreciation against every currency.
Translation and company earnings

Dollar appreciation against a company's revenue currencies can reduce the dollar value of unhedged foreign earnings. The overall effect also depends on costs, hedges, pricing and the currencies involved. Federal Reserve research describes translation and export-competitiveness channels; it does not establish a universal conversion from a DXY percentage move to S&P 500 earnings per share.
A currency worksheet

Suppose a fictional company earns EUR 1 million and has no hedge. At $1.10 per euro, translation gives $1.10 million; at $1.00 per euro, it gives $1.00 million. That $100,000 difference is an illustration for one currency and one unchanged earnings amount. It is not an EPS forecast, and a move in DXY alone does not supply those exchange rates.
Commodities and other influences

For a dollar-priced commodity with an unchanged dollar price, a weaker local currency raises the local-currency purchase cost. In actual markets, commodity prices also change with supply, demand, inventories and interest rates. An inverse relationship with the dollar can appear in a selected sample, but it is not a fixed rule for gold or any other commodity.
Dollar borrowing in emerging markets

A borrower with dollar debt and local-currency income can face a larger local-currency debt-service burden when that currency weakens against the dollar. Dollar revenues or hedges can offset some exposure. BIS research studies broader links between dollar strength and financial conditions; effects vary across economies and periods, so DXY is not an automatic equity signal.
Compare indicators rather than choose one

Read DXY alongside relevant bilateral exchange rates, a broader trade-weighted dollar index, interest rates and the asset's own context. For a study exercise, compare the same dated observations over a chosen interval and report where relationships change. A correlation does not show that the dollar caused another asset's move or predict the next trade.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)
Key takeaways
DXY's euro weight is 57.6%; the basket does not represent every currency.
Earnings effects depend on actual currency exposure, costs and hedging.
Dollar and commodity relationships vary over time.
Dollar debt exposure depends on the borrower's income currency and hedges.
Check your understanding

Dollar appreciation can reduce translated earnings when a company has: Options: No foreign exposure; Unhedged foreign-currency earnings; Only dollar revenue and costs; No earnings. Correct answer: Unhedged foreign-currency earnings. Why: Unchanged foreign-currency earnings translate into fewer dollars if the dollar strengthens against that currency. This is not a universal EPS forecast.

A gold-DXY correlation measured over one period: Options: Guarantees the next price move; Proves dollar moves cause gold moves; May differ in another period; Is always positive. Correct answer: May differ in another period. Why: Correlation depends on the selected sample and does not establish causation or a fixed trading rule.

Which borrower is directly exposed to a larger local-currency burden when its currency weakens against the dollar? Options: One with matching dollar income and debt; One with unhedged dollar debt and local-currency income; One with no debt; Every borrower equally. Correct answer: One with unhedged dollar debt and local-currency income. Why: Currency mismatch can increase the local-currency cost of dollar debt service; hedges or dollar revenues can change that exposure.

Summary

Source-check scope
Source check: 2026-10-18. FRED, BEA GDP and BLS CPI source definitions; no investment-performance validation or professional review.
The four-quadrant regime framework

A four-quadrant worksheet can classify selected observations by whether growth and inflation are rising or falling. Define the measures first: real GDP growth, a survey measure and a monthly release are not interchangeable, and inflation levels differ from changes in the inflation rate. A quadrant is a descriptive simplification, not an asset-allocation rule. Interest rates, starting valuations, supply shocks and expectations can produce different asset returns within the same label.
Building a personal dashboard

FRED provides economic time series and links to their sources and releases. Start a practice dashboard by selecting a few series relevant to a specific question, then record each series' units, frequency, observation date and release date. Check revisions and definitions before comparing values. A dashboard is an aid to study; no measured percentage of useful information or advantage over other traders is established here.
The weekly ritual

For a hypothetical study, choose a review date and record selected yields, exchange rates and price indices. Keep observation dates separate from release dates: GDP is not measured weekly, and later revisions can change the growth story. Record what was actually available at the time. Later revised data can introduce look-ahead bias in a historical analysis; ALFRED archives data vintages where available.
Don't over-trade macro

A macro label cannot determine an appropriate position size or entry time. Scheduled releases can affect prices quickly even when the underlying economic series changes slowly. Compare alternative explanations and unfavorable cases; a dashboard neither proves causation nor guarantees investment outcomes.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)

Growth and inflation can form a four-quadrant descriptive worksheet if the measures are defined.
Record the source, units and dates of each economic series; check revisions before comparisons.
A dated log separates observations from releases and later revisions.
A regime label is not a position-sizing, allocation or timing instruction.

Confirmation bias, anchoring and loss aversion offer ways to examine decisions without assuming a universal emotional response. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
Confirmation bias, anchoring and loss aversion offer ways to examine decisions without assuming a universal emotional response.
Research and individual decisions

Behavioural research studies patterns in how people evaluate uncertain outcomes. Those patterns can help frame journal questions, but they do not diagnose an individual or guarantee better financial results. No level of intelligence or discipline removes market uncertainty.
Confirmation bias

Confirmation bias describes giving more attention or weight to evidence that supports an existing belief. In a practice journal, record the original rationale and at least one observation that would challenge it. Compare how you treated supporting and conflicting information without assuming the exercise removes the bias.
Anchoring

An initial number can influence a later judgement even when it provides little information about current value. A purchase price may become such an anchor. For a worksheet, compare the reasons for keeping a hypothetical position with the reasons for choosing it today; also record costs and constraints. That comparison is a reflection prompt, not an automatic instruction to sell.
Loss aversion and the two-times shorthand

Loss aversion describes losses receiving greater weight than comparable gains relative to a reference point. Tversky and Kahneman's 1992 model estimated a loss-aversion parameter from experimental choices. The familiar 'about twice' shorthand is not a universal measurement of emotional pain. Later studies estimate different magnitudes across people, tasks and methods, and a model parameter should not be treated as an individual trading rule.
A journal exercise

Write down your expected reaction to a hypothetical $100 gain and $100 loss, then describe how the reaction might change with the starting balance or reference point. This exercise observes your reasoning; it does not measure a validated loss-aversion coefficient. A written plan can make decisions easier to review, but it cannot guarantee an exit price or prevent loss. TradeHQ does not execute automatic stop orders.
Recency bias and sample limits

Recency bias can mean giving disproportionate weight to recent observations. A short winning or losing run does not establish a reliable strategy. Compare recent and longer journal periods while noting that market conditions may have changed. No fixed trade count or rolling win-rate window eliminates bias or proves an edge.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)
Key takeaways
Record supporting and conflicting evidence when reviewing a practice decision.
A purchase-price anchor is a reflection prompt, not an automatic exit rule.
Loss aversion varies; the two-times shorthand is not a universal emotional ratio.
Journal samples and written plans cannot guarantee returns or execution.
Check your understanding

Loss aversion describes: Options: Identical reactions from everyone; Giving losses more weight than comparable gains relative to a reference point; Preferring losses to gains; Avoiding all trades. Correct answer: Giving losses more weight than comparable gains relative to a reference point. Why: The concept concerns asymmetric evaluation around a reference point. Its magnitude varies and is not a universal two-times emotional ratio.

Which example illustrates a possible purchase-price anchor? Options: Treating the entry price as the only reason to keep a position; Recording transaction costs; Comparing company revenues; Reading conflicting evidence. Correct answer: Treating the entry price as the only reason to keep a position. Why: An entry price can anchor judgement without establishing current value or dictating whether a position should be kept.

Which journal exercise examines confirmation bias? Options: Record only supporting headlines; Record both supporting and conflicting evidence; Assume a profitable result proves the reasoning; Ignore uncertainty. Correct answer: Record both supporting and conflicting evidence. Why: Comparing how both kinds of evidence were treated can help examine reasoning; it does not guarantee the bias disappears.

Recency bias can lead someone to: Options: Give all observations equal weight; Over-weight the last few outcomes; Ignore all recent evidence; Know the next market move. Correct answer: Over-weight the last few outcomes. Why: Recent outcomes can receive disproportionate weight, while neither a short nor a fixed-size sample proves an edge.

Summary
This lesson examines how frustration or other reactions to recent outcomes may influence decisions; a transaction pattern alone does not reveal someone's emotional state.
What tilt actually is

Tilt describes an emotional reaction to recent outcomes that can pull decisions away from a plan. After a loss, a trader may feel pressure to recover it immediately. That is a prompt for reflection, not evidence that the next trade will win or lose. This lesson uses hypothetical situations and does not rank the causes of account losses.
Notice the urge to change the plan

A useful practice question is whether the next decision follows the original plan or is mainly a response to the last result. Write down any urge to increase size, re-enter immediately or abandon the original rationale. These observations are personal journal notes, not a diagnosis or a reliable prediction of performance.
The revenge trade pattern

A hypothetical sequence is loss, frustration, an unplanned increase in position size and another loss. The eventual drawdown depends on the positions and price changes; no particular percentage follows automatically from that sequence. In a practice journal, compare the intended position size with the size actually submitted.
Concrete circuit breakers

A practice plan can include a chosen daily loss threshold and a pause to review decisions. For arithmetic only, 3% of a hypothetical $100,000 starting balance is $3,000; this is not an industry standard. TradeHQ does not enforce a 3% daily-loss lockout. Its desktop and mobile order panels can show a five-second pause when a proposed trade exceeds 10% of the account balance used by the panel within five minutes of a locally recorded loss. After the pause, the user can proceed or cancel. This is a limited prompt, not a guarantee against further losses.
Recovering from a bad day

For a practice exercise, pause after an unplanned decision and record what changed, why it changed and what you would review before another trade. A plan may specify a break, but no fixed 24-hour interval guarantees emotional recovery or prevents future losses.

An unplanned increase in size changes exposure; this lesson does not rank causes of trading losses.

A Trading Journal: Observations and Limits

Use a decision record to review assumptions without claiming it proves profitable skill. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.
Summary
Use a decision record to review assumptions without claiming it proves profitable skill.
Source-check scope
Source check: 2026-10-18. Editorial check of simulator limitations and referenced U.S. regulator materials; not an expert certification.
What a trading journal can document

A journal is a dated record of choices and the information available when they were made. It may help a learner explain why a simulated transaction was entered and how that reasoning changed. A record by itself does not establish a statistical edge, explain the causes of profits or predict future returns.
Separate a fill record from an interpretation

TradeHQ stores virtual transactions in portfolio history. The user can separately record a hypothesis, alternate explanation, observation time and what would disconfirm the hypothesis. A price marker on a practice chart is not an independent confirmation that a real exchange would execute at that price.
Example: reconcile a practice purchase

Suppose a hypothetical order buys 2 units at $100 each. At a stated 0.1% virtual buy fee, recorded cash decreases by $200.20; the holding has a $200 gross marked value at that price. A later displayed price of $105 would value the 2 units at $210 and show a $10 gross price change. A later hypothetical sale would have additional fees. The exercise is about distinguishing gross and net arithmetic, not a claim about an asset.
Fields worth recording

Possible fields include date and timezone, ticker and instrument type, quantity, observed source and quote age, virtual order price, transaction fee, original question, alternative explanation, and planned review criterion. More columns are not automatically better; use only what serves the learning question.
Review observations, not imagined causes

Grouping past results may reveal a calculation error or a difference between chosen samples. It does not establish that the labels in a journal caused those outcomes. Record unfavorable cases and changes in rules, and avoid interpreting a convenient short sample as proof of a repeatable method.
Sample-size limits

No fixed number such as 30 or 100 decisions proves reliability. Market conditions and dependence between observations matter, as do selection bias, virtual fill assumptions and transaction costs. A journal supports transparent accounting; it does not license larger real-money positions.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)
Key takeaways
A journal is a record, not proof of an investment edge.
Distinguish virtual transactions, observed price marks, interpretation and hypothetical future fills.
Use dated assumptions and include unfavorable observations when reviewing a sample.
No universal observation count validates future performance.
Check your understanding

What can a journal document on its own? Options: A profitable edge; Why the market moved; What observations and assumptions were recorded; A future win rate. Correct answer: What observations and assumptions were recorded. Why: The journal documents information; it does not prove causation or future returns.
In a hypothetical 2-unit order at $100 with a 0.1% buy fee, what cash is spent? Options: $200; $200.20; $210; $0.20. Correct answer: $200.20. Why: The $200 notional plus 0.1%, or $0.20, is $200.20.

Which sample should a review include? Options: Only gains; Only days with stable prices; Only large positions; Favorable and unfavorable cases under recorded rules. Correct answer: Favorable and unfavorable cases under recorded rules. Why: Selecting only attractive cases makes the summary misleading.

Does 30 recorded trades establish a reliable strategy? Options: No universal sample count can do that; Yes, always; Only with a journal; Only if there were no losing trades. Correct answer: No universal sample count can do that. Why: Sample design, costs, dependence and uncertainty matter.
